What a container office is, and what it is not

A container office is a steel office module. We build it on a welded mild steel frame, clad it, insulate it, wire it and finish it inside our works. It arrives as a finished room on a truck. Then you lift it onto a prepared base and connect the power.

That is not the same thing as a shipping container with a door cut into it. Most modules on this page are fabricated from new steel to a container form factor. They borrow the proportions, the corner castings and the handling method. But they do not start life carrying freight.

The difference matters commercially. A fabricated module gives you a clean shell, a known steel history and openings framed where you want them. A converted freight shell gives you the genuine article, with the provenance some clients ask for. Both are honest choices, and we build both.

Six approved layouts, and why width beats length

Every size on this page has an approved general arrangement drawing behind it. Those drawings fix the workstation count, the opening schedule and the partition line before anyone quotes. They are what turns a floor area into an office you can actually staff.

Read across them and one pattern dominates. Internal width, not overall length, sets how many people the module holds.

Why this is a table. Seven variables across six sizes is a comparison a buyer scans, not a passage they read. Written as sentences it would force the reader to hold thirty numbers in memory.

Two rows in that table surprise most buyers. The 20x8 has sixty per cent more floor than the 10x10 and seats one person fewer. Eight feet of internal width cannot take facing desks with a working aisle between them. And the 40x8, at 320 square feet, holds seven workstations where the shorter 30x10 holds twelve, because it loses width and gains a partition.

So a longer module is not automatically a bigger office. If headcount is what you are buying, go wider before you go longer. If the site boundary is what stops you, the narrow sizes exist for that. The drawing tells you honestly what you give up.

Width also changes daylight. At ten feet we can glaze the end walls; at eight feet both ends stay blank and every window sits on the long faces. That is why the 20x10 is described as cross-ventilated and the 20x8 is not.

How the rate moves with floor area

Our rate is calculated from the 20x10 ft module at 200 square feet. Below that size the rate per square foot rises, because the fixed content of a module does not shrink with the floor. A door, a distribution board, a frame and a coating system cost roughly the same at 100 square feet as at 200. Above 200 square feet the rate falls, for the same reason in reverse.

Which container office product actually fits your project

This page sells the standard fabricated office. Four other decisions can pull you off it, and it is cheaper to find that out now than after a quotation.

When the shell has to be a real freight container

Some clients need the freight shell itself. Port and logistics work, client specifications that name ISO dimensions, and projects where the unit may later move as cargo all point that way. That is a conversion, not a fabrication, and it carries its own specification and its own price.

When site duty is the deciding factor

If the module will be lifted, dragged and relocated several times across a project, the build changes. Base rails, lifting points and the coating system all take more punishment. Our site office container is specified for that life, and it is the right answer for a contractor moving offices between phases.

When the value line is enough

Not every office needs the full platform. Some units sit in one compound, house one or two people and never move again. For that job the container office cabin does the work at a lower rate. It is a built cabin. It has no ISO container history, and we never present it as if it did.

When a specialist system replaces the office entirely

Battery storage enclosures, containerised data centre shells, customer-facing marketing offices, multi-storey stacks, flat-pack kits and fold-out expandable units are separate products with separate scopes. If your requirement names one of those, this standard office is the wrong starting point. Ask us and we will point you at the right specification.

How the module is built

Steel structure and the load path

The base is a 150x75x5 mm mild steel C-channel perimeter. It carries the floor, the walls, the transport loads and the reactions at every support point. Inside it we run 100x50x4 mm channels and 80x40x3 mm tubular members as stiffeners, spaced to suit the floor boards and the partitions above them.

The floor frame uses 100x50x3 mm primary members with 80x40x3 mm secondaries. Corner posts are 60x60x3 mm, with 50x50x3 mm intermediates completing the wall frame. The top perimeter is 80x40x3 mm. Roof rafters are 60x40x2.5 mm, with 50x50x2.5 mm purlins across them.

Those numbers matter for one practical reason. Every door, window and service cut-out has to be framed, and the load carried around the opening. An opening is never simply removed from a wall. Move a window after fabrication and the framing has to move with it. So the opening schedule on the general arrangement is worth reading before you order.

Envelope, insulation and finish

Exterior walls are 1.25 to 1.6 mm corrugated MS sheet. The roof is 1.6 mm corrugated sheet, laid to a positive fall with sealed laps and controlled rainwater discharge. Wall insulation is 75 mm mineral wool. Roof insulation is 100 mm glass wool or mineral wool.

Nominal thickness alone does not describe performance. Density, combustibility, vapour control and thermal bridging all move the result, and they are selected against your climate and your project fire strategy. We will not quote a U-value or a fire rating for an assembly we have not tested.

Inside, walls are 12 mm plywood with 0.8 to 1.0 mm laminate. The ceiling is 12.5 mm gypsum or a laminated panel. The floor base is 19 mm marine-grade plywood or 18 mm Bison panel. On top of it we lay 5 to 6 mm SPC or 3 to 4 mm LVT. Externally the module takes a red-oxide primer coat and two anti-rust enamel coats.

Electrical and services

Wiring is concealed PVC-insulated copper. Typical starting sizes are 1.5 sq.mm for lighting, 2.5 sq.mm for sockets and 4 sq.mm for air-conditioning and higher loads. Those are starting values only. Final conductor sizes follow your approved load schedule.

Each module carries a distribution board with MCB and RCCB protection, protective earthing, and segregated lighting, socket and air-conditioning circuits. We provide LED lighting, data points, a UPS provision, 6A and 16A sockets, fan points and a dedicated air-conditioning circuit. Plumbing is excluded unless your approved scope says otherwise.

Standard, optional and excluded: where our scope stops

Most disputes on modular orders start at the boundary, not the build. So we set it out plainly. Standard scope covers the structure, the envelope, the insulation and the internal finish. It also covers the doors and windows on the approved schedule, plus the electrical package described above.

Optional items include air-conditioning, better flooring, security grilles, insect mesh, extra partitions and branding. Custom items include odd-sized openings, heavy-duty coatings for harsh exposure, and any frame change for a special load.

Excluded unless your order states otherwise:

  • Loose furniture and office equipment
  • Transport, unloading, craneage and installation
  • Foundations, plinths and site levelling
  • Site utilities up to the module connection point
  • Statutory approvals and project certification

None of that is a hidden cost. It is a scope line. Tell us which items you want inside the order and we will price them; leave them out and the quotation will say so in writing.

Getting the site ready before the module arrives

A container office needs a level, firm, load-bearing base. Concrete plinths, precast blocks or steel bearers all work. What matters is that the support points sit under the frame where the drawing says, and that the surface is level across the full footprint.

Water is the second thing to plan. The roof discharges rainwater at defined points, so the ground around the module has to take it away. On monsoon-season sites, raise the module enough that the step-up stays usable when the compound turns to mud.

Then check your incoming supply. We deliver the module wired to its board, ready for a single connection. The cable from your site distribution to that point is yours to provide. So is the isolator at it, unless the quotation says we are doing it.

Transport, craneage and site access

Every module in this range travels as one finished unit on a flatbed or low-loader. The 40 ft sizes need the road, the gate and the turning circle that a 40 ft trailer needs. That constraint catches more buyers than any other, and it is worth checking before you choose a size.

Lifting is by crane or telehandler, from the approved lifting points only. We issue the shipped weight, the centre of gravity and the support points before dispatch. Lift from anywhere else and you distort the frame.

Transport, unloading, craneage and installation are quoted separately unless your order says so. Freight in India varies by route, vehicle and season. We would rather price it against your actual site than bury an average in the module rate.

What we check before the module leaves the works

Pre-dispatch inspection covers dimensions, member and sheet identification, welds, coating, roof drainage, weather sealing, doors, windows and electrical continuity. We test the electrical installation for continuity, insulation resistance, polarity and RCD operation.

Punch-list items close before dispatch, not after arrival. Damaged coating is repaired at the works, where it can be done properly. That is the whole argument for factory-built offices, and it only holds if the factory finishes the job.

What to send us so we can quote well

A vague enquiry gets a vague number. Five inputs let us quote properly, and they take about ten minutes to gather.

  • Delivery location and site access width
  • Occupancy: how many people, and what they do
  • Equipment load, including air-conditioning, UPS or servers
  • Whether the module will be relocated, and how often
  • Your required handover date

Send those and your quotation comes back with the inclusions and the exclusions written out. You will not get a rate per square foot that moves at order stage.

Questions buyers ask before ordering

What does a container office cost in India?

Our published rate is Rs 1,450 per square foot at the 200 sq.ft. reference size. A premium applies below that area, and a reduction above it. A 20x10 ft module is Rs 2,90,000 before GST. Those are workbook rates for the standard specification. Your signed quotation sets the final figure.

How many people fit in each size?

The approved general arrangements give four seats at 10x10, three at 20x8, five at 20x10, twelve at 30x10, ten at 40x8 and fifteen at 40x10. Those counts assume the standard workstation size and the standard aisle. Change the furniture and the numbers change with it.

Is this an ISO-certified shipping container?

No. The modules on this page are fabricated to a container form factor. We do not claim ISO 668 compliance, CSC plate approval or stackability for them without project-specific evidence. If you need a genuine converted freight shell, that is a different product and we build it.

Can it be moved again later?

Yes, from the approved lifting points, on a suitable vehicle. Repeated relocation is harder on the base and the coating than a single delivery. So tell us at enquiry stage if the module will move several times. We specify it differently.

What is the warranty?

The warranty period and its exclusions are confirmed in your final quotation. Relocation damage, misuse, site utilities and unapproved alterations sit outside it. Every container office we build carries the same pre-dispatch checks listed above, whichever size you order.

One module or several: configuring a larger office

Four hundred square feet is our largest single module. Above that, you stop buying an office and start planning a layout. There are two honest ways forward, and they behave differently on site.

The first is to place modules end to end. Two 40x10 units give you 800 square feet with a shared entrance deck between them. Still, each unit arrives finished and each lifts on its own. The joint between them needs a weather detail and a level base across both footprints.

The second is to go upward. A stacked build brings in foundations, external stairs, landings, guardrails and structural calculations for the project. That is a different product with its own design scope. So we quote it apart, not as a bigger office.

In practice, most sites reach four modules before a permanent building starts to make better sense. We will say so if your requirement crosses that line. Selling you a sixth container office when a shed would serve you better helps nobody.

How long the module lasts, and what it needs

Life span rests far more on upkeep and exposure than on the build. Coastal air, industrial fumes and standing water all shorten it. Reseal and touch up a module in a dry inland yard and it lasts well. Leave the same unit in a wet corner of a coastal site and it will not.

Three habits do most of the work. Keep the roof drainage clear so water leaves the module instead of sitting on it. Touch up coating damage as soon as it appears, before rust gets under the paint. Reseal around openings after any relocation, because transport moves joints that looked sound.

We do not publish a life-span figure in years. Any number we printed would rest on your site, your upkeep and your exposure, and we cannot check those from here. What we can tell you is the coating system, the steel sections and the sealing detail, which is what actually determines the answer.

New build or refurbished shell: what changes

Buyers often ask if a second-hand shell costs less. It usually does. It also brings trade-offs worth naming first.

A used shell carries a past you did not see. Floor condition, previous cargo, repair welds and existing corrosion all vary between units, so the specification cannot be identical from one order to the next. That is fine on a short-life site office. But it is awkward on a five-year one.

A new module gives you a known steel history. Openings sit where you want them, and the finish matches across every unit in a large order. Where a project needs ten offices that match, that consistency is usually worth more than the saving on a refurbished shell.

What a container office cabin actually is

The phrase covers two different products in the Indian market, and very few listings say which one they are selling. One is a freight container that has finished its shipping life and been converted into an office. The other is a steel cabin built new in a factory, shaped and clad to look like a container. This page sells the second one.

SAMAN builds both. The converted shell is sold as our shipping container office, at a higher rate. A used freight box has to be bought, inspected, cut, reinforced and re-lined. The Container Office Cabin skips that shell entirely. We start with mild steel sections, weld the frame to the size you order, and clad it in corrugated sheet. The result carries the container outline and the flat ISO-profile roof line without carrying a freight certificate.

That distinction is not a marketing point. It changes what you may do with the unit. A freight shell was engineered for stacking and ocean handling, and it keeps that history through a conversion. A fabricated cabin is engineered to stand on a levelled pad, hold an office, and be lifted occasionally by crane from designed points. SAMAN does not claim CSC approval, stacking capacity or freight-container compliance for this product, and no drawing on this page implies any of them.

Fabricated or converted: the decision that moves the price

Most buyers arrive here with a rate in mind and no view on construction. It is worth two minutes, because construction is the largest single variable in the quotation and it is the one nobody publishes.

What you gain by fabricating

You choose the exact external size instead of accepting whatever a 20 ft or 40 ft donor gives you. You get a flat, square interior with no residual shell intrusions where cuts were made and boxed in. Insulation sits inside a purpose-built cavity rather than being furred out from an existing steel wall. Openings land where your layout wants them, because the frame is built around them instead of cut into finished structure. And the rate is materially lower.

What you give up

You give up the freight-grade shell. That means no stacking, no container-handling equipment and no CSC plate. You also give up the heavy corner-casting structure that lets a real container absorb repeated rough handling. If your unit will be lifted onto a truck every few months and set down by a reach stacker, buy the converted shell instead. The higher rate buys handling you will actually use.

How SAMAN builds the cabin, layer by layer

The frame

The base is a 100x50x3 mm MS C-channel platform. Below the floor, a mix of 100x50 mm channels, 50x50 mm angles, 75x40 mm channels and MS square pipes stiffens that platform. Member selection follows the size and the floor layout. The floor grid uses 100x50, 80x40 and 50x50 mm MS square pipes where span and loading require them. The top perimeter is a 50x50x1.6 mm square pipe, and vertical framing uses 50x50x2 mm posts or 60x60 mm MS angles.

Two limits are worth stating plainly. The frame is designed for a single module unless a joined or stacked design is issued separately. The standard floor grid suits workstations and light storage. A heavy safe, a loaded plan chest or a server rack needs local reinforcement, identified before manufacture rather than after delivery.

The envelope

The outer skin is 1.2 mm specially corrugated MS sheet. The roof is 1.4 mm corrugated MS with a factory-formed fall, sealed laps and edge drips that throw water clear of the walls. Wall insulation is 25 mm glass wool or 12 mm Heatlon, and your quotation states which of the two is included. Roof insulation is 50 mm glass wool at a nominal density of 42 kg per cubic metre. The interior lining is 8 mm pre-laminated MDF with aluminium joint sections, and the ceiling uses the same board.

Cut edges, lower laps and opening perimeters are primed and sealed before dispatch. That detail is where a value specification usually fails, so it is worth checking on delivery rather than a year later. Later service penetrations through the roof need proper flashing; cutting one without it is the most common way a dry cabin starts to leak.

The floor

An 18 mm Bison panel forms the deck, fully supported and edge-sealed, with a 1.3 mm vinyl finish laid over it. Vinyl is selected for routine office traffic and easy cleaning rather than for plant movement or pallet trucks. Damaged or wet boards can be replaced without dismantling the cabin, which matters when a unit outlives the project it was bought for.

Openings and services

The standard door is 7x3 ft, outward opening, on a 30x30 mm MS tubular frame, with the door ribs aligned to the wall corrugation. Windows are two-track powder-coated aluminium sliders with 4 mm clear glass. Grills, insect mesh, guards and louvers are supplied only where the approved opening schedule calls for them. Keeping those explicit protects the base rate and lets you buy security where the site actually needs it.

The electrical scope covers a distribution board with MCB and RCCB protection, earthing, and segregation of lighting, socket and AC circuits. Typical conductor sizes are 1.5 sq.mm for lighting and fans, 2.5 sq.mm for sockets and 4 sq.mm for the AC or heavy-load provision. Treat those as starting values. Final conductor size, derating, containment, voltage drop and fault level follow the approved load schedule for your project and the applicable electrical rules.

Comfort is handled by cross ventilation, wall or ceiling fans and a split-AC provision. Outdoor-unit brackets and condensate routing are added once the AC arrangement is confirmed, because both depend on which wall the unit lands against. Plumbing is not included at all in the standard cabin. A pantry or a toilet needs a revised layout, accessible pipework and defined external service connections agreed before manufacture.

Coating and pre-dispatch checks

Corrosion protection is one red-oxide primer coat followed by two compatible anti-rust enamel coats, applied over prepared MS surfaces. Coastal, chemical or heavy-industrial exposure may need an upgraded coating system, and that is priced separately once the exposure category is confirmed. Primer and topcoat compatibility, dry-film thickness, colour, repair procedure and touch-up acceptance are all recorded against your order.

Before the cabin leaves the factory, SAMAN checks dimensions, member and sheet identification, welds, coating, roof drainage, weather sealing, doors, windows, electrical continuity and functional operation. Punch-list items close before dispatch rather than on your site. Ask for that record with the delivery; a value specification is worth what its inspection is worth.

Every size on this page has an approved general-arrangement plan, and each plan publishes its own counts. Buyers who choose on floor area alone usually get one of two decisions wrong, and both are avoidable in about a minute.

A 20 ft by 8 ft body therefore runs a single desk line down one wall. Below ten feet of width, seating is set by width rather than by area, and no amount of extra length changes that.

The second is where the partition appears. Neither 20 ft size carries an internal wall in the approved plan, and neither does the 30x10 ft. The 30x10 ft answers the same need a different way. What the published rate covers, and what it does not

The published rate is a supply price for the finished cabin, ex-factory, before GST at 18 per cent. It covers the frame, the envelope, the insulation, the interior lining and the floor. It also covers the standard door and window schedule, the electrical fit-out described above, and the anti-rust enamel finish in an approved colour combination.

Quoted separately, or excluded

  • Interior fit-out beyond the standard lining, and all loose furniture
  • Transport to site, unloading and craneage
  • Installation, foundations, plinths and levelling
  • Site utilities, including the incoming electrical connection
  • Pantry or toilet provision, and the plumbing that serves it
  • Decorative cladding, complex graphics and premium facade treatments
  • Security grills, insect mesh, guards and louvers, unless the approved opening schedule includes them
  • Project-specific engineering, certification or third-party inspection

Nothing in that list is unusual for this category, and most quotations you compare will exclude the same items. The reason SAMAN publishes it is that most listings do not. A rate that looks twenty per cent cheaper often becomes the more expensive option. Add craneage, a plinth and an incoming connection back in, and the gap closes.

Warranty and service life

SAMAN\'s standard terms are a 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Cover begins at the defined handover milestone. Relocation damage, misuse, unapproved alteration, site utilities, consumables and missed maintenance sit outside it. Design service life is 20 to 25 years under proper use and maintenance, which is a design life and not a warranty period.

Getting the cabin onto your site

Access and lifting

The cabin ships as one welded module and arrives on a trailer. Lifting hooks or lugs are designed to match the completed unit weight, and the unit is handled only from those approved points. Certified slings are required, along with a spreader beam where the lift geometry calls for one. SAMAN issues shipped weight, centre of gravity, support points and a crane plan before dispatch. The site can then plan the lift rather than improvise it.

A 40 ft body is the size that most often catches a site out. It needs trailer approach, turning room and a crane position with clear reach at both lift points. Where the approach is tight, two 20 ft cabins set side by side usually land more easily and cost less to install. They do cost a little more to buy.

What the site must be ready for

  • A level, compacted and drained bearing area at the support points
  • Clear trailer approach and a hard standing for the crane
  • The incoming electrical point positioned before the cabin arrives
  • Agreed positions for the AC outdoor unit and its condensate run
  • Access for resealing inspection after any relocation or major service work

Sites that get these five right take delivery in a morning. Sites that leave the bearing area soft, or the crane standing on fill, lose a day and sometimes a coating.

When this cabin is the wrong choice

It is the wrong choice when the unit will be relocated often, handled by container equipment, or stacked. It is the wrong choice when you need a certified freight shell for customs, port or insurance reasons. It is the wrong choice when the office must carry heavy equipment loads that nobody identified in advance. And it is the wrong choice when a fully serviced toilet block is the real requirement, rather than an office with a provision.

Some site offices move between project phases and interface directly with site services. Our site office container page sets out the specification built for that duty.

What SAMAN needs in order to quote

  • The site location, and the approach available for a trailer and a crane
  • Your preferred size from the six, or the seat count you need
  • Whether a closed manager room is required
  • Any AC, data, UPS or heavy-load requirement, with the connected load
  • Whether a pantry or toilet provision is in scope
  • Your colour preference from the approved palette
  • The delivery date you are working to

With those in hand, SAMAN issues a fixed-price quotation within 48 hours. Standard delivery runs 7 to 21 working days after order confirmation, from the Bengaluru or the Greater Noida factory, whichever serves your site better.

Questions buyers ask before ordering

Is this an actual shipping container?

No. It is a steel office cabin fabricated on a welded MS frame and clad in corrugated sheet. The outline and the roof profile follow a container. If you need a converted freight container, that is a separate SAMAN product at a higher rate.

Can I stack two of them?

Not as standard. The frame is designed for a single module. A stacked or joined arrangement needs a separate design and is not covered by the published rate.

Does the price include a toilet?

No. Plumbing is excluded from the standard cabin. A toilet or pantry needs a revised layout, accessible pipework and defined external service connections agreed before manufacture.

Why does the 20x8 ft seat fewer people than the 10x10 ft?

Because seating is set by width, not by area. Eight feet of internal width will not take facing desks with a working aisle, so the approved 20x8 ft plan runs one three-station line.

What is not included in the published price?

Transport, unloading, craneage, installation, foundations, site utilities, interior fit-out beyond the standard lining, loose furniture, and any project-specific engineering or certification.

How long does delivery take?

Standard delivery is 7 to 21 working days after order confirmation, depending on size, finish selections and current factory load.

What a Labour Colony Is, and What It Is Not

A labour colony is a planned housing site for the people who build your project. It holds several buildings, not one. Typically it has dormitory blocks for sleeping, plus a toilet and bath block. It also has a canteen or mess, a small office, a first-aid point and a security post. Roads, walkways, water, power and drainage tie those parts together.

That last point matters more than buyers expect. Two colonies can hold the same number of workers and still perform very differently. Usually the difference comes from layout, not from the buildings themselves. So this page treats the colony as one system.

You will also see the American spelling, labor colony, in tender documents and on this website\'s address. Both spellings mean the same thing. We use the Indian spelling in our writing because that is how buyers in India say it.

Colony, Camp, Accommodation: The Words Buyers Use

In practice, buyers use several words for the same idea. Some say labour colony. Others say prefab labour colony, labour accommodation or worker housing. All of them describe the same purchase: somewhere for a workforce to sleep, wash and eat near the job.

Two words do mean something narrower, though. A single standalone structure is one building, and it does not become a colony just because workers sleep in it. A camp usually describes a shorter, rougher posting, often in a remote place.

One Building or a Whole Site?

This is the first real decision, so make it early. Ask how long the workforce stays and how many people you must house. Under roughly 40 people for a few months, one building often does the job. Above that, or beyond a year, a planned colony almost always costs less per worker and causes fewer problems.

The reason is simple. One building forces every function into the same box. A colony separates sleeping from washing and cooking, which is better for hygiene, easier to clean and far easier to inspect.

How to Plan a Labour Colony for Your Site

Most published guidance stops at product photos. This section covers the planning we do with buyers before any quotation goes out, because that is where projects go wrong.

Step 1: Fix the Peak Headcount

Start with your peak workforce, not today\'s crew. Almost every site grows, then shrinks near handover. So plan for the busiest month.

Then split that number by trade and by shift. Night-shift workers sleep during the day, so put them in a quieter block away from the road. Supervisors and staff usually need separate rooms, which changes your block mix.

Step 2: Choose Block Size and Storeys

Now match the headcount to block sizes. Our six blocks sleep 58, 86, 115, 129, 142 and 173 people. You can mix sizes freely on one site.

However, height is a real trade-off. A three-storey block houses far more people on the same ground, so it suits expensive or tight plots. But it needs better stair planning, stronger water pressure upstairs and a clearer evacuation route. Two-storey blocks stay simpler to run and are usually quicker to fill and empty.

Depth is then the second trade-off. Five of our sizes are 24 ft deep. The 118x30 ft block is 30 ft deep, so its rooms and its internal passage are wider. Clients who audit worker welfare often prefer that extra width.

Step 3: Place Sanitation, Dining and Admin

Next, position the shared blocks. Keep toilet and bath blocks close to the dormitories, ideally within a short walk, and never place them directly beside the kitchen. Put the canteen where delivery vehicles reach it without crossing the sleeping area.

Your project\'s own rules and your client\'s standards set the sanitation ratios. Those rules decide the seat count, not us. So confirm the applicable ratio before you order, and we will size the sanitation blocks to it.

Admin, first aid and security belong near the entrance. That way visitors, inspectors and ambulances stop before they reach the living area.

Step 4: Plan Roads, Walkways and Utilities

Finally, plan movement and services. Leave a vehicle route wide enough for a fire tender and an ambulance, and keep it clear of parked material. Walkways between blocks should stay usable in monsoon, so plan falls and drainage early.

Utilities then need the same attention. Water storage, pumps, the electrical distribution point, drainage and waste treatment all sit outside the buildings themselves. They form part of your project scope unless your quotation says otherwise. We show them on the layout so nobody assumes they are included.

Choosing Between the Six Colony Block Sizes

Each block above lists its area, bunks and price. This section explains how buyers actually choose.

Usually plot shape decides first. A long, narrow plot suits the 120x24 ft blocks. A compact plot suits stacking upward with the 90x24 ft three-storey block. An awkward plot often works better with two small blocks than one large one.

Next, the programme decides. Short projects favour fewer, larger blocks because there is less to move later. Long projects with rising headcount favour starting small and adding blocks in phases.

Finally, client standards decide. Some clients, especially in oil, gas and public infrastructure, set minimum space per person or minimum room widths. Check those before you fix the block size, because retrofitting is expensive.

A colony rarely uses one size only. A common pattern on a 300-worker site is two 115-bunk blocks plus one smaller block for staff and supervisors.

Mixing Sizes on One Site

Mixing pays off more often than buyers expect. So treat the block sizes as a kit rather than a single choice.

For example, put your general workforce in the largest block your plot takes. Then use a smaller block for supervisors, staff or women workers, who normally need separate accommodation. That approach keeps the main block simple and avoids splitting one building into awkward zones.

Phasing works the same way. Order the blocks you need for the first six months, and leave marked space for the rest. Because the rate per square foot does not change with order size, phasing costs you nothing extra on the buildings themselves.

What a Labour Colony Costs in India

Published prices for worker housing vary wildly, and most listings quote a rate without saying what it covers. That makes real comparison hard. So here is exactly how our pricing works.

How SAMAN Prices a Colony

Every colony block prices on one flat rate: Rs 675 per square foot, before GST. GST applies at 18 per cent. The rate does not change with block size, which is deliberate.

That gives you two useful things. First, your cost per bunk stays roughly steady whether you buy one block or six. Second, you can check any quotation yourself: multiply the built-up area by the rate.

Worked through, the smallest block costs Rs 19,44,000 ex-GST and the largest Rs 58,32,000 ex-GST. Full prices with GST appear against each size above.

What the Price Does Not Include

This matters as much as the rate itself. Our block price covers the building as specified and quoted. It does not automatically include:

  • Land, levelling, foundations, plinths or anchor points
  • External water supply, storage tanks, pumps and distribution
  • Drainage, septic tanks, sewage treatment and waste removal
  • The incoming electrical connection, main panel or generator
  • Internal roads, walkways, boundary walls, gates and lighting
  • Loose furniture, bedding and consumables unless quoted
  • Transport, unloading and craneage unless quoted
  • Statutory approvals, licences and third-party certificates

Some of these we can quote and supply. Others belong to your civil contractor. Either way, your written quotation states which is which, so nothing gets assumed.

Also, we quote freight separately by distance and vehicle. Delivery inside Bengaluru city and across Delhi NCR carries no freight charge.

How the Blocks Are Built

Structure and Envelope

Each block is a newly fabricated steel structure. We do not sell used or refurbished units. The frame uses MS channel, RHS or formed sections, and the final member sizes come from the signed structural drawing for your project.

Walls use GI or PPGI cladding with a liner, or an insulated sandwich panel of PUF, EPS or mineral wool. Panel choice depends on your climate and your project\'s fire brief, so we confirm it per order rather than claiming one build-up suits every site.

Roofing uses insulated PPGI or PPGL sheet, or a sandwich panel roof, with a defined slope, flashing and gutters. Floors differ by use. Dry rooms sit on a steel deck with cement board or an approved slab. Wet areas need an impervious base with proper falls to a drain.

Steelwork gets one red-oxide primer coat and two anti-rust enamel coats over prepared surfaces. Harsh coastal or industrial sites may need an upgraded coating, which we confirm at quotation.

Services Inside the Block

Inside, wiring runs concealed in PVC-insulated copper. Typical circuits use 1.5 sq mm for lighting, 2.5 sq mm for sockets and 4 sq mm for heavier loads, subject to the final load schedule. Each block carries a distribution board with MCB and RCCB protection, proper earthing, and separated lighting, socket and wet-area circuits.

Lighting, fan and socket points are scheduled from the approved electrical drawing for your block, because point counts follow the room layout you sign off. Doors, windows, louvres and mesh follow the same principle: the opening schedule fixes them, not a standard list.

Getting Your Site Ready

Before delivery, your site needs a few things in place. First comes level ground, and each size above lists the area to clear.

You will also need a route that a 40 ft open trailer can reach and turn in. So check low bridges, tight turns and weight limits on the approach road early. Craneage or other unloading equipment must be arranged, because blocks arrive as large assemblies. Beyond that, plan for foundations or pads to the approved drawing, plus water and power to the block boundary.

Monsoon deserves separate thought. Ground that looks firm in April can turn soft in July. So plan drainage, hardstanding and vehicle access for the wet season, not the dry one. Then your colony stays usable all year.

Get these ready in parallel with fabrication. Sites that leave them until delivery week almost always lose time.

What We Need From You to Quote

A fast quotation depends on a few clear inputs. Send us the project location, your peak headcount and the programme dates. Then add the plot size and shape, plus any client standard you must meet.

After that, tell us about access: road width, turning space and whether a crane can reach the position. Finally, confirm which utilities you will provide and which you want us to price. With those in hand, we return a fixed written quotation within 48 hours.

Delivery, Installation and Handover

So we build at Bengaluru for southern projects and Greater Noida for northern ones. Standard delivery runs 7 to 21 working days after order and drawing approval. Assembly on site typically takes 2 to 5 days per block, depending on size and access.

Then, before dispatch, we check dimensions, welds, coating, roof drainage, weather sealing, doors, windows and electrical continuity. You get a fixed written quotation within 48 hours of sharing your site details.

Every block carries a 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Under proper use and maintenance the buildings have a 20 to 25 year design life, which is a design life and not a warranty period.

Related Buildings for Worker Sites

A colony is one of several ways to house a workforce, so it helps to know the alternatives.

If your requirement is simpler and shorter, look at prefabricated labour hutments, which cover basic room-type worker units. If you are housing a crew on a remote or short-duration posting, prefab labour camps address that pattern instead.

Labour Colony FAQs

How many workers can one colony house?

There is no fixed ceiling. One block sleeps between 58 and 173 people, and you can place as many blocks as your plot allows. Colonies we plan commonly range from about 60 to over 500 workers.

Do you build the toilet and bath blocks too?

Yes. Sanitation blocks form part of the colony we plan and supply. The seat and shower count follows the ratio your project or client sets, so confirm that ratio before ordering.

Can the colony grow later?

Yes, and this is worth planning from day one. Leave space on the grid for extra blocks, and size the water and power distribution for the larger future load. Adding a block is straightforward. Resizing a utility spine afterwards is not.

Is land preparation included?

No. Levelling, foundations, plinths and external utilities sit outside the block price unless your quotation says otherwise. We tell you exactly what to prepare and by when.

What about statutory compliance?

Worker accommodation is governed by your project\'s own conditions, by client standards and by the rules applying in your state. Those set your sanitation ratios, space per person and welfare facilities. We build to the standard you confirm, and we ask for it in writing before manufacture.

How soon can a colony be ready?

Blocks deliver in 7 to 21 working days after order and drawing approval, then assemble in 2 to 5 days each. Your civil work and utilities run alongside that, so overall readiness depends mostly on site preparation.

Can we relocate the colony to another project?

Often yes, because the blocks are bolted assemblies rather than cast structures. Relocation needs its own transport, lifting and reinstatement plan, and any damage from moving falls outside the warranty unless separately agreed.

What a labour hutment actually is

A labour hutment is a single prefabricated room, built in the factory and delivered as one piece, in which workers sleep. That is the whole of it. It is not a building with corridors, it is not a block with a staircase, and it is not a camp with its own kitchen. Understanding that boundary is the fastest way to work out whether a hutment is what your site needs, because most of the confusion in this market comes from the word being used loosely for anything temporary that a workforce sleeps in.

The unit arrives complete: frame, walls, roof, floor, door, windows, lights, fan points and a distribution board. It is set down on prepared plinth pads and connected to the site\'s power supply. Workers can occupy it the same week. Nothing about it needs a foundation crew, a mason or a wet trade on site.

Where it sits between a shed and a colony

Three products in the SAMAN Labour Colony range solve three different problems, and picking the wrong one costs money.

A labour shed is one large open enclosure. Everybody sleeps in a single space. It is cheaper per bed at scale and quicker to erect over a big footprint, and it suits a workforce that is uniform, single shift and temporary. If that describes your requirement, the labour shed range is the honest recommendation and this page is not.

A labour colony is a planned settlement: several accommodation blocks plus sanitation, a canteen, an admin office, circulation roads and services, designed together. That is a project, not a purchase, and it is priced and planned as one.

A hutment is the unit in between. One room, one door, four to sixteen beds, standing on its own. You buy one, or four, or eleven, and you place them where the site allows. The reason contractors choose it is granularity. A colony has to be committed to in advance; hutments can be added in the quantity the programme actually turns out to need.

Choosing between GI sheet and PUF panel

This is the only material decision most buyers have to make, and it is worth taking seriously because it is the difference between a hutment people can sleep in through a Rajasthan May and one they cannot.

The budget tier uses profiled GI or PPGI steel sheet with bracing and a liner as specified. It is durable, it is cheap, it is easy to repair with materials available anywhere, and it carries no insulation. In a temperate site, at moderate altitude, or where occupancy is short and seasonal, it is entirely adequate.

The insulated tier uses a nominal 30 to 40 mm PUF sandwich panel. The 40 to 60 mm range is available but is only supplied where the signed bill of materials selects it, so it is not something to assume. The panel changes how the room behaves through the afternoon and overnight, particularly under an uninsulated roof.

Two honest qualifications. First, panel thickness on its own is not a thermal performance figure, and this page does not publish one. The behaviour of the room depends on the joints, the roof, the floor, the openings and the site, not on a single number from a brochure. Second, an uninsulated roof over an insulated wall is a common and expensive mistake. If the site is hot, the roof needs either an insulated panel or an approved radiant or ceiling treatment, and that is priced separately.

How the room is planned

The internal arrangement is deliberately plain, and every element in it earns its place.

Beds and aisle. Bunks stand against the long walls with a clear aisle down the centre. The published occupancy for each size assumes that arrangement. Crowding beds into the aisle raises the headline number and destroys the thing that makes the room usable at three in the morning when someone is coming off shift.

Lockers. Lockable personal storage is what turns shared accommodation from a dormitory into something people will look after. Lockers are itemised separately from the shell price, and it is worth ordering them with the unit rather than later.

Two-room option. From 180 sq ft upward the module can be split into two simple sleeping rooms, each with its own door. Sites use this to house a supervisor separately, or to accommodate a couple, without ordering a second unit.

Cross ventilation, and why the windows face each other

Each hutment carries two openable aluminium sliding windows, and they sit on opposite walls rather than side by side. That is not a styling decision. Air has to enter at one end of the room and leave at the other for the draught to reach the beds in the middle. Two windows on the same wall ventilate the wall, not the room.

Window sill height and bed position are coordinated so a bunk does not stand across an opening and block the airflow the room depends on. Removable mosquito mesh, louvres, privacy screens and protected MS grilles are all available as options, but they are options, and where an opening forms part of the escape strategy a fixed grille must not compromise it.

Ceiling or wall fans are provided as fixed points. A split-AC point is fitted only when it is specifically ordered. The baseline unit is designed around natural ventilation and fans, not sealed mechanical cooling, and a hot or humid site should expect to move to the insulated tier or add cooling after a load review rather than assume it.

Structure, floor and relocation

The frame is welded and bolted mild steel, using IS 2062 or IS 1161 class structural steel or approved equivalent. Member sizes, weld sizes, bolt grades and joint details come from the fabrication drawings for the specific order, not from any nominal schedule, and IS 800 and the project welding requirements are design references rather than a certification.

Two floor options exist and they lead to different products.

The prefab floor uses steel joists carrying an 18 to 24 mm cement, cement-fibre or plywood class board with a vinyl finish. This is the option to specify if the unit may be lifted and relocated. Board edges are supported and sealed, and the assembly is built for sweeping and mopping around beds rather than for wet use.

The fixed floor is a level RCC plinth with screed. It is the better option where the unit will stay put for its whole life, and it removes the joist depth from the step-up at the door.

Relocation deserves a plain warning. A single-piece-lift model and a dismantlable panel model use different connections and different lifting details, and they are identified separately at order stage. Lifting lugs, corner fittings and skid points appear only where the signed general arrangement and lifting drawing show them. A lift plan needs the finished weight, the centre of gravity, the sling geometry and the support points, and forklift handling is permitted only where the pockets and the capacity are documented. Do not assume a unit can be picked up in one piece because a similar one could.

Electrical scope, and what is not in it

Wiring is FR or FRLS copper in approved conduit or trunking, with protected metal penetrations and separation from water, waste and flexible module joints. Typical references are 1.5 sq mm for lighting, 2.5 sq mm for socket circuits and 4 sq mm for air-conditioning or other high-load circuits, but the final cable size is confirmed by the project electrical schedule against the connected load, the voltage drop and the protection coordination. The steel frame and exposed conductive parts are bonded to the tested site earth.

Protection comprises a main isolator, MCB, RCBO or RCCB protection as the design requires, labelled neutral and earth bars, bonding, and surge protection where the supply or the risk assessment calls for it. Wet-area circuits, generator or DG changeover, fault level and the external supply interface all follow the approved single-line diagram. SAMAN supplies and installs to that design; the workbook does not certify the site installation, and the final connection and testing remain a site responsibility.

Fixed lights, fan points, 6A and 16A sockets and exhaust points are provided in the quantities on the approved room and electrical schedule. Loose appliances, air-conditioning units, UPS and data equipment are excluded unless they are itemised.

Sanitation is a separate building

The baseline sleeping hutment has no internal plumbing. There is no attached toilet, no shower and no washbasin unless a basin or pantry point is specifically ordered with its own dedicated supply and waste connection.

This is a deliberate scope boundary, not an omission. Keeping wet services out of the sleeping unit keeps the floor build simple, keeps the cost honest and avoids the hidden drainage work that turns a straightforward order into a civil job. Workers use a separate sanitation or ablution block. If the order does include an attached wet module, the floor changes to a waterproof, sloped, drained wet-area system, and that is a different specification and a different price.

Included, optional and excluded

Included in the published price: the steel frame, walls, roof, floor, one personnel door, two windows, internal lining, fixed lights and fan points, sockets and exhaust points to the approved schedule, the distribution board and protection, the coating system, and factory quality checks with handover documentation.

Optional, priced separately: insulated wall or roof upgrade, ceiling, the two-room split, mosquito mesh, louvres, privacy screens, grilles, a split-AC point, a basin or pantry point, and slip-resistant flooring.

Excluded unless scheduled: bunks and mattresses, lockers, attached toilets, external sanitation, air-conditioning equipment, the civil base and plinth, transport, unloading, site electrical supply, statutory approvals, roads, drainage and every other site infrastructure item.

Site readiness before delivery

The unit arrives complete, but the site has to be ready for it. Before the delivery date, confirm a level, compacted and drained standing area; the plinth pads or plinth beam at the correct levels; clear vehicle access for a trailer and, where a crane is being used, for the crane; an electrical supply point within reach; and a decision on where the drainage apron and the external light point go.

None of that is difficult, but all of it takes longer to arrange than people expect, and a unit that arrives before its base is ready has to be stored somewhere.

Ordering, lead time and what we need from you

Delivery is 7 to 21 working days from a confirmed order, and a fixed-price quotation is issued within 48 hours of a complete enquiry. To price accurately we need the selected size or custom dimensions, the quantity, the wall tier, the delivery location, the required delivery sequence, whether the unit must be relocatable, and whether bunks and lockers are in scope.

SAMAN POS India Private Limited manufactures at Bengaluru and Greater Noida. We are a manufacturer, not a reseller, with over 15 years in prefabricated buildings, more than 500 projects and over 3,000 customers across 15 states.

Warranty is stated identically on every SAMAN product: 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Warranty scope and exclusions are confirmed in the final quotation, and misuse, site services, consumables and unapproved alterations remain outside the agreed scope unless explicitly included.

Maintenance and service life

Design life is 20 to 25 years under proper use and maintenance. That is a design life, not a warranty period, and the difference matters.

What shortens it is predictable: blocked roof drainage, damaged coating at cut edges left unrepaired, sealant failures at penetrations, and relocation damage on units that were moved without a lift plan. Inspect the roof fall and flashing before each monsoon, repair coating damage when it appears rather than at handover, and keep the drainage apron clear.

Labour hutment FAQs

How many workers fit in one hutment?

Between four and sixteen depending on the size, and each size on this page publishes its own figure. The number assumes bunks along the walls with a clear central aisle.

Is there a toilet inside?

No. The baseline sleeping hutment has no internal plumbing. Sanitation is a separate block. An attached wet module can be quoted, but it changes the floor specification.

Can the unit be moved to another site later?

Yes, if it is ordered with the prefab floor and the relocation provisions. Specify that at order stage, because a single-piece-lift unit and a dismantlable panel unit are built differently.

What is the difference between a hutment and a labour shed?

A hutment is one small room for a small crew. A shed is one large open enclosure for a bigger workforce in a single space.

Do I need a concrete foundation?

No. Plinth pads or a plinth beam on level, compacted, drained ground are sufficient for the prefab option. An RCC plinth is used where the unit will stay in place permanently.

Porta Cabin and Portable Cabin: One Product, Two Names

Porta cabin and portable cabin are two names for the same factory-built steel cabin. Construction buyers, contractors and government tenders in India mostly write porta cabin. It is a welded mild-steel chassis with an insulated enclosure, a finished interior and protected electricals. We build it in a factory and deliver it to your site as one module. How SAMAN Builds Every Porta Cabin

Every cabin starts as a welded chassis of 100x50x3 mm MS C-channel with cross stiffeners. The floor is what a cabin lives or dies by, so the chassis gets the heaviest steel. Onto that frame we fix an 18 mm Bison cement-fibre floor board. A 1.3 mm vinyl layer finishes the walking surface. The wall frame uses 50x50 mm MS square pipe with an approximately 60 mm cavity. Outside, the walls carry 1.2 mm specially corrugated MS sheet. Inside, they carry 8 mm pre-laminated MDF lining. The roof runs 1.4 mm corrugated MS sheet over its own stiffener grid.

Insulation is standard, not an upsell. Walls take 25 mm glass wool or 12 mm Heatlon. The roof takes 50 mm glass wool at 42 kg/m\xb3 nominal density, because that is where Indian sun load actually hits. The 7x3 ft MS-framed main door opens outward. Two-track powder-coated aluminium sliding windows carry 4 mm glass. Electricals run in concealed or protected copper wiring on a 1.5/2.5/4 sq.mm schedule. A distribution board with MCB/RCCB protection and earthing controls the circuits. Ventilation is natural cross-flow, with fan, exhaust and AC provisions as scheduled. Plumbing is not included unless your approved scope states it.

Two build facts deserve honest emphasis. First, engineered lifting points are part of the structure, and the cabin is handled only by the approved lifting and support-point drawing. Approximate completed unit weight: 10x10 ft approximately 1.5 tonnes; 20x8 ft approximately 2.4 tonnes; 20x10 ft approximately 3.0 tonnes; 20x12 ft approximately 3.6 tonnes; 30x10 ft approximately 4.5 tonnes; and 40x10 ft approximately 6.0 tonnes. These are approximate completed unit weights, not floor load capacity, roof load capacity, lifting capacity or structural load capacity. Actual completed unit weight can vary with the approved configuration, fit-out and optional equipment. The cabin is designed to be moved, and that is what makes it genuinely portable rather than merely prefabricated. Second, the final colour, openings and fit-out follow your approved drawing. The images on this page are approved SAMAN visualisations of the standard build, not a fixed appearance. The complete line-by-line specification sits in the Specifications tab and in the versioned PDF.

What Buyers Use Porta Cabins For

Site and project offices are the largest use. A contractor orders the cabin with the work order, and the office lands before the first excavation. General-purpose rooms come next: security points, drivers\' rooms, first-aid rooms, storage and sample rooms. Retail and service use covers shops, kiosks, ticket counters and reception units, usually in the shop configuration. Sanitation and project-support configurations round out the family, from toilet-fitted cabins to stores.

The common thread is time. Civil construction of a 200 sq ft room takes months and leaves debris. A porta cabin arrives finished, works the same day it is placed, and moves to the next site when the project ends. That reuse is also why buyers who once rented often switch to owning.

Porta Cabin on Terrace and Rooftop

Rooftop placement is one of the most asked questions on this page. It often works, because the module weighs far less than an equivalent masonry room. Two checks decide feasibility. First, your structural engineer must confirm the slab can carry the cabin at the planned position. Second, there must be crane or lifting access to the roof level.

Share the building height, slab details and access photos with your enquiry. We then advise on the lift plan and quote accordingly. However, never place a cabin on a roof without the engineer\'s confirmation. That check is the buyer\'s responsibility, and we state it plainly.

The published price buys the standard open-room specification. Almost everything else is configurable. CUSTOM work covers layouts, colours and openings, which follow your approved drawing. Cheap quotes usually hide in the specification, not the price. Compare line items, and the differences surface fast. Ask every vendor for the same five numbers:

  • Chassis section and thickness (ours: 100x50x3 mm MS C-channel)
  • Wall and roof sheet thickness (ours: 1.2 mm and 1.4 mm corrugated MS)
  • Insulation type and thickness in walls and roof
  • Electrical protection (DB with MCB/RCCB and earthing, or a bare board)

Porta Cabin FAQs

What does a porta cabin cost per square foot?

The published band runs from ₹1,187.50 to ₹1,437.50 per sq ft ex-GST, depending on size. The 20x10 ft cabin at 200 sq ft works out to ₹1,250 per sq ft. Compare the published price for each standard size in the table and request an itemised quotation for the configuration you need.

What sizes does a porta cabin come in?

Six published sizes: 10x10, 20x8, 20x10, 20x12, 30x10 and 40x10 ft, all 8.5 ft high. Send your requirement with your enquiry if none of the six matches your footprint.

Can a porta cabin be installed on a terrace or rooftop?

Rooftop or terrace placement depends on the building. Ask your structural engineer to confirm that the slab can carry the cabin at the planned position, and check that there is lifting access to roof level. Share the building height, slab details and access photos with your enquiry.

Do I need a foundation?

The base is set by the project engineering approved for your order, and any base work is outside the published price. Share your site conditions with your enquiry so the base requirement can be confirmed for your location.

How long does delivery take?

Standard delivery takes 7–21 working days from confirmed order, plus transit. Your quotation confirms the schedule that applies to your order.

Is GST included in the published prices?

Prices are shown ex-GST with the 18% inclusive figure alongside, under HSN 9406 for prefabricated buildings.

How long does a porta cabin last?

Service life depends on use, siting and maintenance. Warranty period and exclusions are confirmed in the final quotation for your order.

Can I customise the layout?

Yes. Partitions, furniture, AC provision, colours and openings follow the drawing approved with your order. Send your requirement with your enquiry and it will be quoted against that drawing.

The Heavy Industrial Build in the SAMAN Porta Cabin Range

Every porta cabin family needs one build that treats the cabin as plant, not furniture. In the SAMAN range, that build is the MS Porta Cabin. It uses the strongest mild-steel profile in the porta cabin cluster. The frame is IS 2062 Grade A industrial steel. The shell is 1.6 mm-class corrugated sheet on both walls and roof. The floor is a rigid 24 mm-class build-up. This specification serves plant compounds, EPC projects, workshops and other demanding fixed-position duty, where the cabin works through one long deployment rather than moving between short ones.

The name deserves one honest sentence. MS simply means mild steel, the carbon steel that Indian fabrication runs on. When buyers search for a steel porta cabin, this mild-steel build is almost always the product they mean. This page therefore covers both names with one published specification, one price ladder and one quotation process. Every number here traces to SAMAN\'s controlled costing and specification workbook. The downloadable PDF in the hero carries the same data under a document version you can hold us to.

That traceability is the practical difference between this page and a directory listing. A listing shows a price and a photograph. This page shows the sections, thicknesses and scope boundaries behind the price, so your comparison starts from evidence rather than adjectives.

Inside the Build: Frame, Shell, Floor and Insulation

The chassis is the heart of the specification. A 100x50x3 mm MS C-channel primary base frame, ISI-standard or approved equivalent, forms the load-bearing foundation of the cabin. Bottom stiffeners use 100x50 mm C-channels, 50x50 mm MS angles, 75x40 mm channels and approved square-pipe supports. Their spacing is coordinated at about 4 ft intervals to the final floor load and lifting design. On that grid sits an 18 mm cement-fibre floor board fixed with approved self-tapping fasteners. The floor builds up to its 24 mm class and takes a 2-3 mm commercial PVC, epoxy or 3 mm chequered-plate finish.

The frame above follows the same industrial logic. Corner and wall posts use 50x50x2 mm MS square pipe, or an approved 60x60 mm MS-angle alternative. Door and window openings are reinforced, and the wall cavity runs approximately 60 mm. The top perimeter is 50x50x1.6 mm square pipe. Roof stiffeners of 50x50x1.2 mm carry secondary members sized to span, ceiling support and drainage slope. Walls and roof both carry 1.6 mm corrugated MS sheet. For comparison, the standard porta cabin uses 1.2 mm walls and a 1.4 mm roof. The MS build runs heavier metal exactly where site abuse lands.

Inside, the lining is chosen for punishment rather than polish. Interior walls take 8-10 mm fibre-cement board or a 0.50 mm pre-painted metal liner. The ceiling matches, with 8 mm fibre-cement or metal lining. Both options tolerate impact and moisture better than decorative boards do. Thermal duty is covered by 50-75 mm mineral wool in the walls and 75-100 mm in the roof, where Indian sun load actually strikes.

The result is a shell that holds its interior through years of plant service. Welded and bolted connections follow approved shop drawings. Edges are deburred, dimensions inspected, and panels closed only after the frame passes inspection. Final engineering, the bill of materials and the drawings remain controlled documents, issued with your order rather than improvised at the factory.

MS, GI or Pre-Galvanized: Choosing Your Steel

Steel porta cabins are specified in three material routes, and the right one depends on your site, not on a sales pitch. Mild steel protected by a maintained coating system is the standard industrial choice for inland and normal-humidity sites. Galvanized iron adds a zinc layer for sustained humidity. Pre-galvanized sheet is coated before fabrication, for the most exposure-critical panels. The table below states the practical selection logic in one view, because material questions are the ones buyers most often get conflicting answers on.

Steel routeBest-fit siteWhat it changes
MS (this page)Inland, dry and normal-humidity industrial sitesStandard heavy build; approved primer/topcoat system maintained through life
GI (galvanized)Coastal, high-humidity and long-exposure sitesZinc-coated steel for corrosion duty — see the GI Porta Cabin page
Pre-galvanizedExposure-critical panels on aggressive sitesSheet coated before fabrication; specified per project at quotation

The honest guidance is simpler than the market makes it. If your site is inland and your duty is heavy, the MS build on this page is the specified answer. Its coating system is part of the published specification, not an extra. If your cabin will serve on the coast, near brine or in permanently humid air, read the GI Porta Cabin page instead, which owns the galvanized configuration in this range.

State the site environment in your enquiry, and the quotation names the material route we recommend for it. We quote the route the site needs, not the costliest one that sounds safer. Whichever route you pick, the cabin sizes, layout options and quotation process on this page stay the same.

Where the MS Build Earns Its Cost

The MS Porta Cabin earns its premium over the standard build wherever the cabin works as part of the plant. Typical deployments run through cement, steel, power and process plants: gate and weighbridge control rooms, shift offices beside running lines, instrument and panel rooms, and sampling stations. EPC and infrastructure contractors specify it as the resident site office that must outlast a multi-year contract. Workshops use it as a supervisor cabin and records room inside fabrication bays, where trolleys, material and the occasional impact are daily facts.

The common condition in all of these is fixed-position service under industrial exposure: vibration nearby, material movement around the shell, sun on the roof for years. Layout stays flexible inside the open single-room baseline. Partitions and furniture follow your approved drawing, and ventilation runs from natural cross-flow with fan, exhaust and AC provision as the schedule requires.

Where the requirement is a light office for a short project, the heavier steel is not the economical answer, and we say so plainly. In that case, the standard build in the porta cabin range serves better. Duty decides the build; size then decides the price.

Corrosion Protection, Service Life and Maintenance

Mild steel lasts as long as its protection system, so the specification treats coating as structure. Prepared MS surfaces receive the approved primer and topcoat system, matched to substrate and exposure category. Cut edges and fabrication damage are repaired before dispatch. The final colour is project-selected and confirmed in the finish schedule. That is why the photographs on this page show different finishes rather than one catalogue colour.

Under proper use and maintenance, the service life of the build is 20-25 years. That is a design-life statement, not a warranty period. The standard warranty is 5 years structural and 1 year finishing, extendable to 2 years on request and confirmed at quotation. Maintenance is ordinary industrial practice: keep the coating intact, attend to damage promptly, and keep roof drainage clear.

Quality is checked before dispatch, not argued after delivery. Pre-dispatch QA covers dimensions, member and panel identification, connections, coating, roof drainage, weather sealing, doors, windows, electrical continuity and functional checks. Corrosion-compatible fasteners and EPDM, butyl or approved sealants close every panel joint, corner, roof lap and penetration, and no unsealed field cut is accepted.

Scope: What Is Standard, Optional, Custom and Excluded

The published price buys a defined industrial specification, and the boundaries are stated rather than discovered at delivery. STANDARD scope covers the IS 2062 Grade A frame, the 1.6 mm corrugated enclosure, insulation, lined interior, floor and finish. It includes a heavy MS main door with an industrial lockset, in single or double leaf. Windows are reduced-size aluminium units or louvered ventilators with 5 mm glass, where the opening schedule uses them.

The electrical baseline is complete rather than token. Protected copper wiring runs on a 1.5/2.5/4 sq.mm starting schedule, controlled by a distribution board with MCB/RCCB protection and earthing. LED lights, modular switches and 6A/16A sockets are fitted as scheduled. Final circuit quantities and equipment loads follow the approved electrical drawing and your quotation.

OPTIONAL additions include AC provision and units, exhaust and ventilation fittings, grills, mesh and guards, and furniture or partition packages. CUSTOM decisions cover the layout, openings and colour, all finalized by your approved drawing, because the open single-room baseline is deliberately a starting point. EXCLUDED scope is equally explicit. Plumbing and sanitary work are not included unless your approved scope shows them. Transport, installation, foundations and project engineering are quoted separately. Options never silently become standard, and the quotation lists each one as its own line.

Delivery, Lifting and Site Readiness

Your fixed-price quotation arrives within 48 hours of sharing requirements. Standard delivery takes 7-21 working days from confirmed order. Cabins dispatch from the nearer factory, Bengaluru for the South and Greater Noida for the North, on 20 ft or 40 ft open trailers priced by the distance ladder in the Shipping tab. Delivery within Bangalore city and the listed Delhi NCR areas is free. Every module carries engineered lifting and handling points. Move the completed module only to the approved lifting, support and transport drawing.

Because the MS build is the heaviest cabin in the porta cabin range, arrange the crane and confirm approach access before the trailer arrives. If the cabin will move between sites repeatedly as a planned duty, tell us at enquiry. The Skid-Mounted Porta Cabin is the configuration built around repeated relocation, and it may fit that duty better. Send these details with your enquiry, and the first quotation arrives ready to compare:

  • Site location pin code, and whether access suits a 20 ft or 40 ft trailer
  • Cabin size and duty, with the rooms or zones you need inside
  • Door, window and ventilation positions, if already decided
  • Electrical load expectations, including AC and equipment points
  • The base you will prepare: compacted ground, plinth or columns
  • Target delivery date, and the person authorised to receive the module

MS Porta Cabin FAQs

Is an MS porta cabin the same as a steel porta cabin? In practice, yes. MS means mild steel, and the mild-steel build is what steel porta cabin almost always refers to in the Indian market. Galvanized and pre-galvanized variants are the exceptions, and each is specified separately in this range.

What does an MS porta cabin cost? The published ladder runs from ₹1,29,375 for 10x10 ft to ₹4,27,500 for 40x10 ft ex-GST, on a ₹1,125 per sq ft base rate at the 20x10 ft reference size. Interior fit-out, transport and installation are quoted separately.

What steel grade does SAMAN use in the frame? The frame is specified in IS 2062 Grade A mild steel, the Indian structural standard for general engineering, in an ISI-standard or approved equivalent C-channel chassis.

How long does an MS porta cabin last? Service life is 20-25 years under proper use and maintenance, with the coating system kept intact. The warranty itself is 5 years structural and 1 year finishing, extendable to 2 years on request.

Can I use an MS porta cabin on a coastal site? We recommend the galvanized build for sustained humidity or salt air. Mild steel with a maintained coating serves inland sites well, but zinc protection is the right specification near the coast.

Can the cabin be relocated later? Yes. Engineered lifting points are part of the structure, and the module relocates by crane and trailer to the approved handling drawing. For duties that involve repeated planned moves, the skid-mounted configuration is purpose-built.

Is plumbing included in the MS porta cabin? Not by default. Plumbing and sanitary work appear only when your approved scope shows them. If the cabin needs a washroom, say so at enquiry, and the quotation prices that scope as its own line.

What a GI Porta Cabin Is, and When You Should Specify One

A GI porta cabin is a factory-built portable cabin in which the weather-facing steel is zinc-coated rather than only painted. Zinc protects steel sacrificially. At cut edges, scratches and fastener points, the zinc corrodes first. The base metal underneath stays shielded. So the shell survives handling damage that starts rust on ordinary painted sheet. That single property decides where this cabin earns its price.

Specify GI when the site itself attacks steel. Coastal yards and ports live with salt-laden air. Process plants place cabins beside cooling towers, wash bays and chemical stores. Hill and high-rainfall locations keep surfaces wet for weeks. Remote sites cannot schedule repainting at all. In each case, a painted-only shell demands maintenance the site cannot easily give. A zinc-coated system keeps protecting between rare inspections.

SAMAN builds GI porta cabins at two factories: Bengaluru for South India and Greater Noida for the North. Delivery to site takes 7–21 working days. The company has manufactured portable buildings since 2009, was incorporated in 2019, and has delivered 500+ projects across 15+ states. Every cabin leaves the factory only after a pre-dispatch inspection. That check covers dimensions, coating, roof drainage, weather sealing, doors, windows and electrical continuity.

Three Galvanized Builds and Why Your Quotation Must Name One

Most Indian listings sell a \\"GI cabin\\" at one per-square-foot rate without saying what is actually galvanized. Three different builds hide behind that label. They perform differently, and they price differently. SAMAN quotations name the route explicitly, so you can compare offers on substance.

In the full-GI route, the 100x50x3 mm structural channel chassis and the frame members are hot-dip galvanized to an approved schedule. Welded and cut locations are repaired with a zinc-rich system, and certificates travel with the cabin. The hybrid route protects the members that trap moisture first. The cladding route relies on the zinc-coated skin alone; the frame stays painted MS. Many fabricators quietly sell that third build as \\"GI\\". Ask the question before you compare prices.

The Specification Details That Decide Corrosion Life

Thickness alone tells you little about a galvanized sheet. Corrosion life follows the zinc coating mass, in grams per square metre, on a given base-metal thickness. SAMAN wall cladding uses 0.8–1.2 mm BMT corrugated GI/PPGI to IS 277 or approved equivalent. The project schedule states both the BMT and the required coating mass. Steel mills publish GI capability from 0.13–3.0 mm with coating up to 275 gsm. So the specification you sign matters far more than the word \\"galvanized\\" in a listing.

The roof uses 1.0–1.4 mm BMT profiled zinc-coated sheet with sealed laps and flashings. Roof framing keeps positive drainage, because standing water defeats any coating. Interiors default to a 0.40–0.50 mm pre-painted metal liner rather than MDF. Board materials swell in persistently damp service; fibre-cement board remains available where you prefer a board finish. The floor pairs a protected steel cross-grid with 18–24 mm cement-bonded board. Offices get 2 mm commercial vinyl on top. Rough industrial duty gets 3 mm chequered steel.

Small components break corrosion systems, so they get the same attention. Fasteners are corrosion-compatible with the zinc-coated shell. Joints, corners, roof laps and penetrations carry EPDM, butyl or approved sealants. No unsealed field cut is accepted. Aluminium window frames are isolated from dissimilar steel and perimeter-sealed. Door hardware matches the shell\'s coating strategy, and threshold details prevent water trapping at the opening.

Condensation is the quiet failure mode in humid climates. The cabin manages it as one system. Walls take 50–75 mm mineral wool or 50 mm PUF/PIR infill with climate-specific vapour control. The roof takes 75–100 mm mineral wool or a 60–80 mm insulated panel. Ventilation moves moist air out, and AC condensate is routed clear of the chassis and cladding. If insulation performance drives your decision more than corrosion does, the PUF porta cabin is the sibling built around that priority.

Where GI Porta Cabins Go to Work

Ports and shipyards use them as gate offices, tally rooms and stevedore rest cabins, because salt air is constant and repainting halts operations. Fisheries and aquaculture units place them beside processing halls, where washdown keeps everything wet. Chemical and fertiliser plants stand them near storage areas that painted steel cannot tolerate. Desalination and coastal power projects order them for long construction phases in the spray zone.

Inland, the case is humidity rather than salt. Breweries, dairies and food plants run high-moisture halls. Pharma sites need cabins beside wash bays. Hill-state projects in Kerala, the Konkan belt and the Northeast face months of monsoon wetting. Mining and tunnel sites add condensation from temperature swings. For each of these, the GI build trades a known one-time premium for years of avoided repainting and downtime. Contractors who redeploy cabins between projects buy GI for the same reason. A module that moves every year cannot count on gentle weather at its next site.

Two honest boundaries help you buy correctly. First, GI is a corrosion decision, not a security or fire decision. If your need is fire rating or acoustic control, other cabins in the range own those jobs. Second, a dry inland compound rarely justifies the premium. SAMAN will say so in the quotation rather than sell coating you do not need.
