What Is Standard, What Is Optional, What Is Excluded

STANDARD in every GI porta cabin: the zinc-protected structure and cladding for the quoted route, insulated walls and roof, metal-liner or fibre-cement interior, cement-bonded floor with vinyl finish, one office door, sealed aluminium windows, and complete wiring with LED lights, modular switches, 6A/16A sockets and a protected distribution board. Pre-dispatch QA and the coating documentation for the quoted route are part of the product, not extras.

OPTIONAL at order: extra windows or louvers in place of windows, security grills and mosquito mesh, fan and AC provision, chequered-steel flooring for rough duty, partitions for cabin-plus-store layouts, and plumbing with sleeved, sealed penetrations. Each option appears as its own line in the quotation, so you can drop it without re-pricing the cabin.

CUSTOM work such as non-ladder sizes, project-specific coating schedules and laboratory fit-outs is engineered to order and priced case by case. EXCLUDED unless your quotation says otherwise: foundations, statutory approvals, site power supply, plumbing connections, unloading equipment and freight. The exclusions are printed because surprise scope is the most common complaint buyers carry from previous cabin purchases. A quotation that lists what it does not include is the one you can actually compare.

Maintenance and Service Life in Corrosive Service

A GI porta cabin under proper use and maintenance offers a 20–25 year service life. That is a design expectation, not a warranty period. The standard commercial cover is a 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty, with the finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request and confirmed at quotation. Relocation damage, misuse, site services and unapproved alterations sit outside that scope.

Maintenance in corrosive service is light but specific. Inspect annually. Wash salt deposits off external surfaces. Check sealant lines at roof laps and penetrations. Touch up coating damage with the approved zinc-rich repair system, never ordinary paint. Keep the underside ventilated and drained, because trapped water under the floor defeats the protection strategy faster than rain on the walls. Full-GI cabins ship with their coating repair procedure, so your site team knows the correct material before the first scratch happens.

Can I mix a galvanized frame with standard panels? Yes. The hybrid route galvanizes the chassis and critical members while the rest of the build follows the standard specification. It suits humid industrial sites that want structural protection without the full-GI premium.

Noise is the one site condition you cannot design around by moving a desk. A cabin thirty metres from a diesel genset still sits in the same sound field as one three metres away. It is just further down the curve. What changes the experience inside the room is the construction of the box itself. This page sets out how SAMAN builds that box. It covers what each layer does, where performance is usually lost, and what we need from you before any number goes against it.

What "soundproof" means on a SAMAN quotation

We use "soundproof" as the product name, because that is what buyers search for and ask for. We do not use it as a physical promise. We will not put a decibel figure on a page where the assembly has not yet been defined.

The reason is simple. Sound reduction is a property of a complete installed assembly, not of a material. The same wall build-up measures differently depending on the door fitted into it. The glazing beside it changes the result. So does the ventilation path, the sealing of the services, and the care taken when the module is set down and closed up. A number quoted against the wall alone tells the person in the room very little.

So the sequence runs: you state the target, we design the assembly against it, and the target is verified on the completed installation. Some projects need a numeric figure committed contractually. In that case we quote it only against a defined test or measurement method. Any door or glazing carrying a rating must carry a published test result of its own. This is a slower conversation than a headline figure. It is also the only one that survives contact with a real site.

The mass-spring-mass build, layer by layer

The strategy behind the cabin is mass-spring-mass. Two masses separated by a soft layer work far better than the same material laid up as one solid slab. Every part of the cabin is a version of that idea.

Mass on the outside

The external shell is a 1.2 to 1.6 mm corrugated MS or PPGI skin. The roof skin runs 1.4 to 1.6 mm. This shell does the weather job and provides the outer mass. Panel seams, corners and service penetrations are all sealed. At the frequencies that matter, a small continuous gap can dominate the result of the whole wall.

Absorption in the cavity

The cavity carries 75 to 100 mm of stone or mineral wool. The roof and ceiling cavity is filled continuously. Our reference material is a stone wool of the ROCKWOOL Safe n Silent type. The manufacturer publishes it as non-combustible with an A1 classification and a thermal conductivity of 0.033 W/mK. Density and thickness are then chosen for the specific wall system.

It is worth being precise about this layer. Cavity insulation damps resonance inside the cavity. On its own it does not set the transmission performance. Copy across this category often implies that thicker insulation means better isolation. In practice, skins, spacing, decoupling, seals, openings and installation quality all matter more.

A decoupled lining on the inside

The internal lining is where the design earns its cost. It uses two 12.5 mm board layers, or an equivalent mass lining. Joints are staggered so no single line runs through both layers.

The lining rides on resilient channels or on independent inner studs. It is not screwed hard to the structural frame. That keeps the inner leaf from being rigidly bridged to the outer skin at every member. Where the target allows a rigid connection, cost comes down. Where it does not, the lining support stays separate, and the design says so. Structural posts are a 60x60x3 mm reference and the top frame an 80x40x3 mm reference. The lining does not simply hang off them.

Floor and ceiling

The floor is an 18 to 24 mm rigid board or dense barrier over a resilient underlay, on an engineered steel grid. The finish is a 2 to 3 mm resilient vinyl, rubber or carpet tile over acoustic underlay where the duty allows. It is chosen for impact noise as much as for wear. Where the system requires it, perimeter isolation stops the resilient finish short-circuiting into the wall frame.

The ceiling is a multi-layer board on resilient channels or hangers, with a sealed perimeter. Every light, diffuser and access panel is a hole. Each one is gasketed and sealed rather than simply cut.

Two structural points follow from all this. They are why an acoustic cabin is not a standard cabin with extra insulation. First, the bottom frame is a 150x75x5 mm MS C-channel reference, sized by mass and load calculation for the actual lining package. It is not copied across from a lightweight office cabin. Second, the 100x50x3 mm cross-members control floor deflection and carry the resilient floor layers.

Doors, glazing and the openings that decide the result

In practice the weakest element sets the outcome. That element is almost always an opening.

The door is a solid-core or acoustic door set with perimeter seals. Where the target requires it, an automatic or drop threshold is fitted. Leaf, frame, hardware and seals are selected together. A door closing onto a compressed seal on all four edges behaves very differently from the same leaf on a standard frame with a gap under it.

Glazing is sealed laminated or double glazing. A 6/12/6 mm build-up is a starting point for discussion and nothing more. Real selection uses asymmetric glass thicknesses, laminated interlayers, a considered cavity and properly sealed frames. All of it is matched to the frequency spectrum you actually have. A crusher, a genset and highway traffic do not present the same spectrum. Glazing that suits one is not automatically right for another. Where a project needs a rated result, we set the specification with an acoustic consultant or the glazing manufacturer.

Security grills, mosquito mesh, guards and louvers are fitted only where the approved opening schedule calls for them.

Ventilation without an open sound path

A sealed room still needs air. Cut a plain vent through an acoustic wall and you have built a direct path for the noise you just paid to exclude.

The cabin therefore uses a duct attenuator, an acoustic louver or a baffled air path. The air turns corners and passes absorptive surfaces, and the sound loses energy on the way. Fan vibration, duct breakout noise and condensate penetrations are treated as part of the acoustic design. They are not left as separate mechanical items. Air conditioning provision is coordinated with the approved layout, and the load is quotation-specific.

Services, penetrations and the gaps that dominate

Electrical and plumbing work is where a good acoustic wall is quietly undone.

Boxes are staggered rather than mounted back to back across a partition. Pipes are sleeved and carried on resilient supports. Every penetration is sealed with an acoustically compatible system. Rigid service bridges across a high-isolation partition are avoided. A single hard connection can carry structure-borne sound straight past the layers designed to stop it.

The electrical scope itself is conventional and follows the approved drawing. The starting schedule is 1.5 sq.mm for lighting, 2.5 sq.mm for sockets and 4 sq.mm for higher-load or air conditioning circuits. A distribution board carries MCB and RCCB protection, earthing, and segregation between lighting, socket and air conditioning circuits.

Where an acoustic cabin earns its cost

The configuration suits any place where people must work, concentrate or talk inside a noisy environment rather than away from it:

  • Site and project offices inside an active construction compound rather than at the gate
  • Control rooms and operator positions near crushers, compressors, pumps and generator yards
  • QA, measurement and inspection rooms where ambient noise interferes with the work
  • Meeting and briefing rooms on plants, ports and highway projects
  • Offices facing a highway, a railway line or a boundary shared with industry
  • Rooms where the need runs the other way, and activity inside should not carry to neighbours

Reverberation is a different problem from transmission

Two buyers describe the same complaint in the same words and need opposite solutions.

Transmission is sound getting in or out through the envelope. Reverberation is sound bouncing around inside the room once it is there. It is why a hard-surfaced meeting room feels tiring even when the meter says it is quiet. The mass-spring-mass build addresses transmission. Reverberation is handled with absorptive surface treatment inside the room, specified separately.

If your problem is that people on a call cannot be understood, say so at enquiry. The answer may be internal treatment rather than a heavier wall.

Choosing between the six sizes

Six sizes are published. The specification is costed against the 20x10x8.5 ft reference at ₹1,650 per sq.ft. The other five derive from that input through the area-band adjustment. That is why the rate per square foot falls as the unit grows.

On coastal or chemically aggressive sites, corrosion may outrank the acoustic question, and the galvanized iron porta cabin is the better starting point. The full porta cabin range shows how the configurations compare.

Site readiness and delivery day

An acoustic module is heavier than an equivalent standard cabin, because the mass is the point. That has consequences on site.

The position needs level, compacted hardstanding that can take the module without differential settlement. A frame that racks will open the seals you paid for. Access has to suit the approved transport and lifting drawing. A 40 ft unit needs a clear route, turning space, and a set-down position the crane can reach. Lifting and support points are engineered and marked, and the module moves only to that drawing.

Closing up matters just as much. Perimeter sealing at the base, at any module joint and around every service entry is part of the acoustic work. It is not a finishing detail.

What we need in order to quote an acoustic target

A useful quotation needs the acoustic problem described, not just a size:

  • The noise source, its distance from the cabin position, and whether it runs continuously or in bursts
  • The internal condition you need to hold, as an NR or NC value if you have one, or in plain terms if you do not
  • Any contractual Rw or STC requirement, and the method it will be judged against
  • Occupancy and use: single desk, team office, control room, meeting space
  • Ventilation and air conditioning needs, plus any equipment that will run inside the room
  • Site access, crane availability and the set-down position
  • Whether any equipment inside the cabin vibrates, which needs separate isolation design

Call out heavy vibrating equipment early. Inertia and isolation design for machinery is a separate exercise. It is not assumed in the standard cabin price.

Delivery, warranty and service life

SAMAN POS India Private Limited manufactures under the SAMAN Portable brand. Our factories are in Bengaluru and Greater Noida, so units for southern and northern projects are built at the nearer plant. The company was founded in 2009 and incorporated in 2019, with over 15 years of experience. We have a team of over 200, and more than 500 projects and 3,000 customers across over 15 states. We manufacture rather than resell.

A fixed-price quotation is issued within 48 hours of a complete enquiry. Delivery runs 7 to 21 working days, depending on size, configuration and the current build queue. Office hours are Monday to Saturday, 09:00 to 20:00 IST. GST is 18% and the HSN code is 9406.

Warranty is stated as follows: 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Service life is 20 to 25 years under proper use and maintenance. That is a design life, not a warranty period. Warranty scope and exclusions are confirmed in the final quotation. Relocation damage, misuse, site services, consumables and unapproved alterations sit outside the agreed scope unless explicitly included.

Common questions

Can you tell me the dB reduction before I order?

Not honestly, no. Reduction is a property of the finished assembly, including the door, the glazing, the ventilation path and the site sealing. Tell us the target and the method it will be judged by. We will design and price against it.

Is a soundproof porta cabin the same as an acoustic enclosure for a machine?

No. An acoustic enclosure wraps equipment. This is an occupied building. It has to handle ventilation, daylight, access, services and comfort at the same time as sound, which is a different design problem.

Does more insulation mean better sound reduction?

Not by itself. Cavity insulation damps resonance in the cavity. The isolation comes from mass, separation, decoupling and sealing working together.

Will it also be cooler, and quieter in rain?

The stone wool that does the acoustic work also insulates thermally. Published conductivity for the reference material is 0.033 W/mK. Rain noise on the roof is a separate matter. It may need extra damping or an insulated panel roof, specified case by case.

Can the cabin be relocated later?

Yes, it is a transportable module. Move it only to the approved lifting, support and transport drawing. Expect the perimeter and service seals to be inspected and made good at the new position.

Do you provide acoustic testing?

Testing is not included in the standard price. Where a project needs laboratory or field evidence, we arrange and quote it separately. Any numeric claim is then tied to that defined method.

Fire safety requirements reach site cabins later than they reach buildings, but they do reach them. A permit office beside a tank farm will face the question one day. So will a document room inside a process plant, or a site office in a warehouse full of combustible stock. A fire consultant will ask what the cabin actually does in a fire. This page explains how SAMAN answers that question: with a specific build, published planning prices and honest scope.

What Fire-Rated Actually Means on a Porta Cabin

A fire rating is not a property of a material name. It belongs to a complete tested assembly. That means a specific wall build-up, a specific door set in a specific frame, and a specific sealed penetration, each supported by test evidence for that exact construction. A supplier who prints 60 minutes or 120 minutes on a website, without naming the tested system, is quoting a number without a certificate.

SAMAN takes the opposite position. Your project states the required fire-resistance period and reaction-to-fire criteria. Those usually come from its fire strategy, consultant or tender specification. We then specify the wall, roof, ceiling, door and penetration systems whose test evidence matches those criteria. Your quotation lists that documentation item by item. The cabin is sold as fire-rated only when the tested systems behind it are confirmed for your order.

This approach costs us easy marketing lines. In return, you get a cabin whose paperwork survives an audit. Factory fire officers, EPC document controllers and procurement teams can file the quotation, the material certificates and the test evidence together, and every claim in that file traces to a source.

Where This Configuration Earns Its Premium

The fire-rated build costs more than a standard steel cabin of the same size, and the premium buys specific things. It buys a non-combustible envelope instead of a conventional one. It buys door sets that are tested products rather than fabricated gates. It buys penetrations that are sealed systems rather than open cut-outs. Buyers who need those things usually know it already, because a consultant or a tender clause has told them.

Typical placements include hot-work permit offices near fuel and chemical storage, control and document rooms inside process plants, site offices in high-value warehouses, and cabins procured under tender clauses that state fire criteria. If none of that describes your site, a standard cabin serves you better and costs less. We would rather route you to the right product than sell you the wrong premium.

How SAMAN Builds the Fire-Rated Configuration

The build starts from the same heavy MS platform that carries our industrial porta cabins. The envelope, linings, openings and services then change around fire performance. Nineteen of the thirty technical line items in this product\'s specification are unique to the fire-rated configuration.

Structure

The chassis uses a heavy MS primary frame with a 150x75x5 mm C-channel reference section. Secondary support comes from 100x50x3 mm channels and engineered cross-members. Corner posts are 60x60x3 mm SHS with reinforced rated openings. The 80x40x3 mm top frame carries protected connection zones, so wall and ceiling junctions stay continuous where the tested system needs them to be. Every unit gets engineered lifting points. Qualified fabricators weld or bolt the structural connections to approved shop drawings.

Envelope and linings

Exterior walls use 75-100 mm mineral-wool sandwich panels with 0.5-0.8 mm pre-coated GI or GL facings. The roof is a mineral-wool roof panel or a tested non-combustible roof build, with insulation continuity maintained across joints. Inside, walls take 12.5 mm fire-grade gypsum, calcium-silicate or fibre-cement layers as the certified system requires. The ceiling assembly stays continuous where partitions meet it. Stone and mineral wool is the insulation family throughout. Where your project specifies that level, we use an A1-class product; ROCKWOOL publishes Euroclass A1 reaction-to-fire data for its Safe n Silent Pro range.

Foam-core panels tell you why this matters. PUF and EPS cores insulate well and cost less, and they serve our other cabin configurations honestly. Their fire behaviour, however, depends entirely on density, facings and the tested assembly. A fire-focused specification starts from non-combustible stone wool instead.

Floor

The floor build avoids combustible board as the default. A steel floor grid carries 18-24 mm cement-bonded board or an engineered cementitious deck. The finish is a commercial resilient or epoxy system, chosen from documented low-flame-spread options where the project requires them. The adhesive and skirting follow the same documentation rule as the finish, because a floor system is only as good as its weakest documented layer.

Doors, windows and openings

The main door is a tested fire-door assembly: certified leaf, frame and hardware with a self-closer and seals as required. Its rating matches your project fire strategy, not a catalogue default. Windows are the honest difficulty in any fire-rated cabin, and we say so plainly. Standard aluminium windows with ordinary glass are not fire-rated. Rated walls therefore either omit glazing or use a certified fire-rated glazing system where one is permitted. Grills, mosquito mesh and louvers appear only where the approved opening schedule allows them.

Services and penetrations

Electrical work follows the platform standard. Concealed or protected copper wiring runs on a 1.5, 2.5 and 4 sq mm starting schedule, with final sizing by load. A distribution board provides MCB and RCCB protection with earthing. LED lights, modular switches, 6A and 16A sockets and fan or AC provision are coordinated on the drawing. What changes in the fire-rated build is everything that passes through a rated boundary. Ventilation and AC penetrations take tested dampers or fire-stopping where the strategy requires them. Cables, pipes and conduits pass through tested penetration seals rather than open cut-outs.

Detection and suppression deserve one honest sentence. Detectors, extinguishers and alarm systems belong to your project\'s fire strategy and its licensed contractors. What to Put in Your RFQ

A fire-rated enquiry moves fastest when it arrives with the facts a specifier needs. Include these points and the quotation comes back precise instead of provisional:

  • The required fire-resistance period and criteria, and who stated them (consultant, tender, factory officer)
  • Cabin size from the six-size ladder, plus your room layout if partitions are needed
  • Door and window schedule, marking which openings sit in rated walls
  • Site location and access notes for freight and placement
  • Electrical load points and AC requirement
  • Required delivery date

If the rating requirement is still undefined, say so. We will quote the base fire-resilient build and mark the rating-dependent items as options. That keeps your budget honest while the fire strategy catches up, and nothing gets bought twice.

Standard production runs 7-21 working days from confirmed order. A fixed-price quotation reaches you within 48 hours of a complete enquiry. Cabins ship complete from our Bengaluru and Greater Noida units. Freight follows the published trailer ladder: a 20 ft open trailer starts at Rs 25,000-30,000 for the 100-150 km band, and a 40 ft trailer at Rs 30,000-35,000, with each further 50 km band adding roughly Rs 5,000. Delivery inside Bengaluru city is free. So is delivery across Delhi NCR, including Ghaziabad, Gurugram, Faridabad, Noida and Greater Noida. The 12 ft wide sizes move as over-dimensional cargo, and their route charges are confirmed once the delivery location and order are fixed. Transport charges may shift slightly with route and vehicle return.

Your site needs a level, load-bearing base, clear crane access for placement and a power point for hook-up. Engineered foundations and statutory sign-off, where a project requires them, remain in your scope. We state that in the quotation rather than discovering it at delivery, because surprises at the gate cost both sides money.

Quality Checks, Warranty and Support

Every cabin passes a pre-dispatch inspection before it leaves the factory. The checks cover dimensions, member and panel identification, connections, coating, roof integrity and functional tests of doors, windows and electrical circuits. SAMAN POS India Private Limited operates ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015 and ISO 45001:2018 certified management systems. The company has delivered 500+ projects across 15+ states from its two manufacturing units.

The commercial warranty reads the same on every SAMAN page because it comes from one controlled source: 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Relocation damage and site modifications sit outside warranty scope. For certified fire assemblies, the final quotation governs warranty terms.

Service life is a separate number from warranty, and we keep the two apart deliberately. A well-maintained steel cabin of this class delivers 20-25 years of service under proper use and maintenance. That figure describes expected life, not a warranty period. Maintenance itself stays simple: keep drainage paths clear, touch up coating damage early, and have any repair that touches a rated wall, door or seal carried out to the same documented system it came with.

Relocation is part of this product\'s value. Engineered lifting points are standard, and the cabin moves by crane and trailer as one unit. After any relocation, inspect door seals, panel joints and penetration seals before the cabin returns to duty, because the certified build only protects a room when its assemblies sit as tested. Relocation damage sits outside warranty scope, so plan the lift with competent riggers.

One boundary note helps some buyers. If your requirement leans toward acoustic performance rather than fire criteria, the same mineral-wool family serves a different specification in our soundproof porta cabin. Genuinely mixed requirements are best resolved in one engineering conversation. For standard configurations and the full size range, start from the porta cabins range and compare against your site needs.

Frequently Asked Questions

What fire rating does the cabin carry?

The rating your project specifies. We build to certified assemblies whose test evidence matches your stated fire-resistance period and criteria, and the quotation lists that documentation. We do not publish a blanket minutes figure, because no honest manufacturer can rate a cabin before knowing the required systems.

Is the cabin fireproof?

No cabin is. Fireproof is a marketing word; tested assemblies resist fire for defined periods under defined conditions. If a supplier offers you a fireproof cabin, ask for the test report and watch the claim change.

Can I add windows wherever I want?

In non-rated walls, yes, from the standard window schedule. In rated walls, glazing is either omitted or supplied as a certified fire-rated glazing system where permitted. An ordinary aluminium window would defeat the wall it sits in.

Do you supply fire detectors and extinguishers?

Those systems belong to your project\'s fire strategy and its licensed contractors. We build in the provisions, brackets and interfaces your layout calls for, and we hand over a cabin ready to receive them.

How fast can one reach my site?

Production runs 7-21 working days after order confirmation, plus freight time by the published trailer bands. Quotation turnaround is 48 hours from a complete enquiry. The 12 ft wide sizes add route confirmation time for over-dimensional movement.

What a PUF porta cabin actually is

A PUF porta cabin is a transportable building whose walls and roof are factory-made sandwich panels rather than a frame with insulation added inside it. Each panel arrives as one finished element. It carries a pre-coated steel skin outside, a rigid polyurethane foam core in the middle, and a second pre-coated steel skin inside. That inner skin becomes the visible wall surface of the room.

That single sentence carries most of the difference. In a framed and lined cabin, insulation is a layer inside a shell, and the interior finish is a separate material fixed over it. Here the insulation, the weather skin and the interior finish are the same component. The steel structure underneath still does the structural work. Its sizing follows what the chosen panel can span rather than what a cladding sheet needs.

The standard planning build uses 50 mm wall panels and 60 to 80 mm roof panels. Facings are pre-coated GI or GL in the 0.5 to 0.8 mm range that the panel industry typically supplies. We offer an 80 mm wall panel where a project needs higher insulation. The chassis is a 100 x 50 x 3 mm MS C-channel reference frame. The floor sits on an MS cross-grid and uses an 18 mm cement-bonded board, with a 24 mm option for higher duty.

Where the panel build earns its money

Rooms people occupy through the summer

The clearest case is a room somebody sits in all day, in a place that gets genuinely hot. A continuous insulated envelope with sealed joints cuts the heat reaching the inside face. It also cuts the air leakage that makes an air-conditioned cabin expensive to hold at temperature. Site offices, control rooms, testing rooms and any cabin with instruments or people in it for a full shift are the honest applications.

Space that has to look finished immediately

Because the panel inner face is the finished wall, a PUF cabin does not need a lining trade on site. There is no MDF to fit, no joint to fill, no surface to paint before anyone moves in. A cabin delivered on Tuesday can be occupied on Tuesday. For marketing offices, client-facing site offices and anything a visitor will walk into, that matters as much as the thermal performance.

Interiors that need a wipeable surface

The pre-coated steel inner face is a hard, smooth, cleanable surface. That suits rooms where dust, handling or hygiene expectations make a soft lining a liability. This is not a clean-room specification and we do not claim one. The base surface simply starts from a better place than a board lining.

The envelope, layer by layer

Wall panels: 50 mm standard, 80 mm option

Fifty millimetres is the standard planning thickness. The published price ladder costs against this thickness, and it suits most site offices in most Indian conditions. Eighty millimetres is the documented higher-insulation option. Specify it when the cabin faces long solar exposure, when air-conditioning load drives your operating cost, or when the room must hold temperature with plant running outside.

Thickness is a planning decision, not a performance certificate. Core density and thermal conductivity come from the panel supplier\'s certificate for the system you actually buy, and the purchase order names them. We publish no conductivity figure or U-value for the cabin. A cabin figure would have to account for the frame, the joints, the openings and the installation, and none of that is fixed until the design is.

Roof panels: why the range is 60 to 80 mm

The roof gets more thickness than the walls for a simple reason. It takes the most direct solar gain, it spans further, and it has to carry drainage and any service loads. The factory roof panel gives you weather skin, insulation and finished underside in one element. Its outer skin is profiled and its inner liner arrives finished.

Where the roof lands inside the 60 to 80 mm range depends on heat gain, on the span the design needs, and on condensation requirements. The panel supplier\'s structural and thermal data governs the allowable span and the fastener spacing. We therefore coordinate the roof secondary members to the panel rather than assume them. These are typically 50 x 50 x 1.2 mm and engineered as the span requires.

Facings, joints and why sealing decides the result

A good panel installed with poor joints performs like a poor panel. The controls that matter are unglamorous. We use interlocking joint profiles, corrosion-compatible mechanical fasteners, EPDM or butyl or approved sealants, and flashings at joints, corners, roof laps and every penetration.

We accept no unsealed field cut. Every cut edge exposes the core, and an exposed core is where water, vapour and time get in. Where a cut has to happen, we close it with the approved flashing and sealant detail before the panel passes inspection.

The steel under the panels

It is worth being explicit about this, because the panel is the visible part and it is easy to assume it does everything. It does not. The transport and lifting chassis remains structural steel, and we size it independently for cabin loads and for handling. Panel fasteners never substitute for structural connections.

The reference build uses a 100 x 50 x 3 mm MS C-channel bottom frame. Stiffeners in 100 x 50 and 75 x 40 channel and square pipe support the floor loads and the panel perimeter rails. A 50 x 50 x 1.6 mm MS SHS top frame gives the wall panel heads a straight, level bearing. Wall framing is 50 x 50 x 2 mm MS SHS, with framed openings locally reinforced.

That last point has a practical consequence. Large openings need local reinforcement, and we design that reinforcement in rather than cut or crush the panel core to get it. A wide window or a double door is a structural decision taken before manufacture, not an adjustment made later.

Lifting and handling points are engineered provisions. We move a completed module only to the approved lifting, support and transport drawing. We weld or bolt structural connections to approved shop drawings, deburr and inspect edges, and close panels only after the frame passes inspection.

Services: planned before manufacture, never cut in later

This is the single discipline that separates a PUF cabin that lasts from one that disappoints, and it is the thing most buyers are never told.

You cannot route services by cutting channels through a sandwich panel. Doing so removes core, breaks the vapour path and leaves an unsealed edge inside the wall where nobody will ever see it fail. So we settle the service strategy before the panels are made.

In practice that means:

  • Wiring runs in planned chases and raceways, or in surface containment, rather than in improvised cuts.
  • Copper wiring follows the standard starting schedule: 1.5 sq.mm for lighting, 2.5 sq.mm for sockets, 4 sq.mm for higher-load or air-conditioning circuits. The load schedule and the approved electrical drawing set the final sizes.
  • We provide a distribution board with MCB and RCCB protection, earthing, and segregation of lighting, socket, wet-area and air-conditioning circuits, to the approved drawing.
  • Plumbing, where you order it at all, uses factory-planned sleeves and chases. We seal every penetration and protect the core, and we plan service zones and removable covers before manufacture.
  • We plan air-conditioning sleeves and condensate drains at the factory, so we restore insulation and vapour sealing around each penetration rather than patch it later.

Final quantities of lights, switches, sockets, fan points and air-conditioning provision stay quotation-specific, and we coordinate them with the approved layout. We do not publish fixed counts, because a count that is right for one layout is wrong for the next.

Condensation, ventilation and air conditioning

An insulated, well-sealed box behaves differently from a leaky one, and that is mostly the point. It also means the ventilation strategy has to be chosen deliberately rather than left to the gaps.

We select the ventilation approach for occupancy and climate. It may use natural ventilation through the opening schedule, or air conditioning with controlled condensate. What it must not be is uncontrolled vapour movement through panel joints, because that is how moisture reaches places it cannot dry from.

Where a false or service ceiling is added below the insulated roof, it creates a void for services. It does not replace the roof panel\'s thermal function, and the vapour and condensation control has to stay continuous above it. That distinction is easy to lose on site and expensive to rediscover later.

What a PUF panel does not do

Two limits deserve stating plainly, because the market around this product is not always honest about them.

The first is fire. Fire resistance cannot be inferred from PUF thickness. A thicker PUF panel is a better insulator; it is not a fire rating. Where a project requires a non-combustible core, the answer is a tested mineral-wool panel system rather than more polyurethane. That is a different build with a different specification. If fire performance is what your project is actually buying, start at the fire-rated porta cabin instead of specifying this one and hoping.

The second is that a panel is not a structure. The chassis carries the building. The panel closes it, insulates it and finishes it. Treat with suspicion any claim that a sandwich panel cabin needs less steel because the panels are strong.

Choosing between 50 mm and 80 mm

The honest guidance is narrower than most buyers expect.

Specify 50 mm for a normal site office in normal conditions. It suits cabins where air conditioning runs during working hours rather than continuously, and cabins you expect to relocate within a few years. This is the standard build, and the published prices cover it.

Specify 80 mm where solar exposure runs long and unshaded, or where the room must hold a set temperature against a continuous heat load. It also earns its cost when air-conditioning running cost over a multi-year deployment is a real line in your budget, and on semi-permanent cabins.

Specify neither on the basis of a number you found on a competitor\'s page. Panel data belongs to the panel you actually buy, and the supplier issues it as a certificate against that purchase order.

A PUF cabin asks for the same site preparation as any other module in the range, with two additions worth planning for.

Prepare a level, load-bearing base with drainage away from the cabin footprint. Pedestal or plinth support at the designed positions matters more here than on a framed cabin. A module that sits out of level puts the panel joints out of line, and joints out of line do not seal as designed.

Keep the panel faces protected during offloading and positioning. A pre-coated skin is the finished surface, so a gouge is not a scratch on a cladding sheet, it is damage to the finished wall. Touch-up is possible, and we match the corrosion protection system to substrate and exposure, but prevention costs nothing.

Pre-dispatch quality checks cover dimensions, member and panel identification, connections, coating, roof drainage, weather sealing, doors, windows, electrical continuity and functional checks. We verify specialist performance certificates where the product requires them.

The final quotation confirms warranty period and exclusions. Relocation damage, misuse, site services, consumables and unapproved alterations sit outside the agreed scope unless the quotation explicitly includes them.

What we need in order to quote accurately

A PUF cabin quotation moves faster when these are settled at enquiry:

  • Footprint and quantity, and whether the cabin is a standalone module or part of a linked set.
  • Wall panel thickness, 50 mm or 80 mm, and whether the roof sits at 60 mm or 80 mm.
  • Any nominated panel system or brand, or confirmation that we may propose one.
  • Opening schedule: door type and position, window sizes and positions, and any framed structural opening.
  • Service requirements: lighting and socket layout, air-conditioning provision and sleeve positions, and whether plumbing is in scope.
  • Floor duty, so we can confirm 18 mm or 24 mm base and the finish.
  • Site access, approach width, offloading arrangement and the delivery location for freight.
  • Colour and coating preference, and whether the cabin is a short deployment or semi-permanent.

Anything we cannot confirm from that list stays a quotation input rather than a website claim.

Questions buyers actually ask

Is a PUF cabin cooler than a standard site office? A continuous insulated envelope with sealed joints reduces heat transfer and air leakage, and buyers report that as a more comfortable room. We publish no temperature difference. The honest answer depends on orientation, glazing, ventilation, occupancy and the air-conditioning system, and the design fixes none of those until it is complete.

Can I get a U-value or a thermal conductivity figure? For the panel you actually buy, yes, from the supplier\'s certificate, and the purchase order names it. For the finished cabin as an assembly, that needs a defined calculation or test method covering the frame, joints and openings. We quote a cabin figure only against such a method.

Is PUF fire resistant? No, not by virtue of being PUF, and not more so because it is thicker. Where a project requires a non-combustible core, a tested mineral-wool panel system replaces PUF.

Can I cut a new opening after delivery? Not without a designed detail. We protect the core, then seal and flash the cut edge, and larger openings need local reinforcement. Tell us at enquiry if a future opening is likely.

Does the interior need painting? No. The panel inner face is the finished surface. A decorative or hygienic lining is a separate order if you want one.

Is the 80 mm option worth it? It is worth it for long solar exposure, continuous temperature holding, or a multi-year deployment where air-conditioning running cost matters. For a normal site office on a normal programme, 50 mm is the specification we would recommend.

What a Double Story (G+1) Porta Cabin Is, and When It Pays

A double story (G+1) porta cabin is a stacked modular building. The factory builds two cabin modules, and an engineered chassis, stacking columns and inter-module connections turn them into one two-floor structure on site. You get a ground floor, an upper floor and an external steel staircase, all on the plot area of a single cabin.

The buyer problem it solves is simple. Most working sites run out of ground before they run out of people. Vehicle lanes, material yards, cranes and stores claim the plot first. Meanwhile the team still needs offices, meeting rooms, records rooms and rest rooms. The G+1 build takes the one resource the site still has: the air above an existing cabin footprint.

So the page ahead answers the four questions G+1 buyers actually ask. First, when stacking beats buying two separate cabins. Second, what changes structurally, because a stacked cabin is not two standard cabins placed on top of each other. Third, what each of the six sizes really decides. Fourth, what the published price covers and what the structural quotation adds.

The Ground Area Maths: One Footprint, Twice the Rooms

Work the numbers before you choose. A 20x10 ft cabin gives 200 sq ft of rooms on 200 sq ft of ground. Two of them give 400 sq ft of rooms but consume roughly 500 sq ft of plot once you add the gap and walkway between units. The G+1 version gives the same 400 sq ft of rooms on the original 200 sq ft plinth.

The table below puts the two routes side by side, because this single comparison decides most G+1 purchases.

Decision factorTwo single storey cabinsOne G+1 porta cabin
Ground area usedRoughly 2.5x one cabin footprintOne cabin footprint
Plinth and base workTwo plinths, two levelling jobsOne plinth, one levelling job
Team separationTwo doors across the yardTwo floors, one staircase apart
Structural scopeStandard single storey practiceProject structural calculation
AccessGround level onlyExternal stair, guards and landing

Read the last two rows carefully. The stacked route saves ground but adds engineering scope and stair access. That trade is worth it on tight plots. It is unnecessary on open ones, which is why we say so plainly in the orientation section above.

What Changes Structurally From a Single Storey Cabin

Here is the honest engineering core of this product. A single storey cabin never carries another building on its roof. A G+1 ground module does, so SAMAN re-engineers the load path from top to bottom rather than reusing single storey members.

The ground floor chassis becomes a two-storey transfer chassis. Its reference starting section is a 150x75x5 mm MS C-channel, which is substantially heavier than a standard cabin base. Transfer members and base stiffeners line up under the stacking posts of the upper module. Corner columns become stacking columns, with a 60x60x3 mm SHS reference section in place of standard single storey posts, and each module carries a reinforced ring beam that moves vertical and lateral loads into the stacking connections.

The upper floor deserves its own paragraph, because it is the most misunderstood part of a stacked cabin. It is not a roof with flooring laid over it. It is an engineered structural floor, checked for live load, deflection and vibration, with a 24 mm cement board or heavy deck walking surface. Only the top module carries the weather roof, with a positive slope and sealed penetrations. The lower module top is treated as inter-storey construction instead.

One rule ties all of this together. Every section named above is a reference starting section, and the final member sizes, foundation reactions, wind and seismic stability, connection plates and anchors come from project structural calculations. SAMAN publishes the reference sections so you can compare vendors honestly, and releases fabrication only against the approved structural package. Treat any G+1 quotation without that calculation step as incomplete.

Stairs, Access and Egress Are Engineered Scope

The staircase is part of the structure, not an accessory. Stair clear width, riser geometry, handrails, guards, landings and escape routes are set by the approved egress plan for your occupancy, and the stair, landing and guard steel is designed with the building. Doors on occupied floors open outward as the egress plan requires, and upper floor access is coordinated with the stair and landing system.

Openings follow the same discipline. Windows and service openings cannot cut stacking posts, transfer members or required bracing, so large openings get reinforcement shown on the approved shop drawings. If a layout sketch shows a window where a stacking column stands, the drawing changes before fabrication, never on site.

Services Floor by Floor

Each floor runs its own services. Electrical wiring follows the protected copper schedule of 1.5, 2.5 and 4 sq.mm circuits with a distribution board, MCB and RCCB protection and earthing, engineered per floor to the approved load schedule. Ventilation and air-conditioning run floor by floor as well, with sealed service risers and no uncontrolled openings between storeys.

Plumbing stays excluded unless you order it. When you do, wet areas stack vertically where practical, so risers, vents and drainage stay short and serviceable, and every floor penetration receives waterproofing treatment as required. Decide toilets and pantries at drawing stage; they are simple to align between floors on paper and expensive to relocate after fabrication.

Six Sizes and the Published Planning Ladder

SAMAN publishes the full six-size ladder, because a G+1 buyer deserves a working budget figure before the structural quotation arrives. Every figure below is a planning estimate derived from the published rate input of Rs 1,310 per sq ft and the area band adjustments, and the area basis is the total built-up floor area across both floors. What Buyers Put on Each Floor

The most common configuration is office over office: supervision and visitor handling below, engineering, documentation or management above. Plants and campuses also run office over store, keeping ground level for material receipt while records and quality teams sit upstairs. Marketing and administration setups use the upper floor for meetings, since visitors experience the stair once and the ground floor keeps daily traffic.

Know the boundary of this product as well. A single G+1 cabin serves one team or two, up to the 1,200 sq ft flagship. Project-scale worker housing with rows of rooms, kitchens and ablution blocks is a different product family, and our labour colony pages cover those G+1 and G+2 accommodation blocks with their own capacity planning. Residential living layouts belong to the porta cabin house instead. Keeping those boundaries clear protects your specification and your budget.

Scope: What Is Standard, Optional, Custom and Excluded

STANDARD scope covers the engineered stacked structure: transfer chassis, stacking columns, both floor structures, the top-storey weather roof, insulated envelope, interior lining, doors and windows per the approved opening schedule, the external stair package and the per-floor electrical baseline.

OPTIONAL scope covers partitions, furniture, air-conditioning units, stacked wet areas with the vertical plumbing riser, grills and mesh, and extra doors or windows where the structure allows them.

CUSTOM scope covers layouts, colours, cladding selection and opening positions, always through the approved drawing. EXCLUDED scope covers foundations, transport, unloading, site power supply and project-specific engineering and tests, which are quoted separately once your site details are known. Every option lands as a line item on the quotation, so you can add or remove scope and watch the effect.

Transport, Unloading and Site Readiness

A G+1 cabin travels as separate modules and becomes a two-storey building during installation. Modules up to 20 ft ride a 20 ft open trailer, and 30 to 40 ft modules ride a 40 ft open trailer, with freight following the distance ladder in the Shipping tab. The 12 ft wide modules of the 40x12 ft size can classify as an over-dimensional consignment, and ODC charges stay estate-dependent until the route is confirmed.

Prepare the site before the trailers arrive. You need a level base built to the approved foundation drawing, clear approach and turning room for the trailer, working space for the crane during stacking, and a power point for the distribution board hook-up. Anchoring follows the structural package. The staircase side needs its clear strip, so mark it on the plinth plan from day one.

What Your Structural Quotation Needs From You

Send these inputs with your enquiry, and the 48-hour quotation comes back with the structural scope already framed: your site pin code and city, the intended use of each floor, expected occupancy per floor, preferred footprint from the six-size ladder, any heavy equipment or storage loads, known wind exposure or rooftop placement plans, and whether you need stacked wet areas. Soil information helps early when you have it, because foundation reactions from the G+1 structure drive the base design.

Our range works from two owned factories, in Bengaluru for the South and Greater Noida for the North, and you can compare this stacked configuration with every other build in the porta cabins range before you commit.

How to Compare G+1 Quotations Line by Line

Cheap stacked-cabin quotes hide their savings in the structure, and you cannot see the structure in a photograph. So compare quotations on five numbers before you compare prices. Ask every vendor for the transfer chassis section under the ground module, and compare it against our published 150x75x5 mm reference. Ask for the stacking column section, against our 60x60x3 mm SHS reference. Ask what the upper floor is designed for, because a converted roof and an engineered floor look identical in a render and behave differently under a loaded file rack.

Then ask two scope questions. Does the quotation include project structural calculations, foundation reactions and an approved drawing set, or does it reuse single storey members without a check? And is the stair package, with guards, landings and egress geometry, inside the price or left as a site extra? A vendor who cannot answer these five points in writing is not quoting the same product. Ours are printed here, in the Specifications tab and in the versioned PDF, so you can hold the delivered building to the promise.

Why Buy the G+1 From SAMAN

SAMAN POS India Private Limited, brand SAMAN Portable, was founded in 2009 and incorporated in 2019, which gives you over 15 years of manufacturing experience behind the stacked build. Two owned factory units, in Bengaluru and Greater Noida, serve the South and North directly, so you buy from the manufacturer rather than a reseller. The delivery record stands at 500+ projects for 3,000+ customers across 15+ states, executed by a 200+ member team, with ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015 and ISO 45001:2018 certifications and NSIC SPRS registration. Working hours run Monday to Saturday, 09:00 to 20:00 IST.

Quality, Warranty and Honest Limits

Every module passes pre-dispatch QA covering dimensions, member and panel identification, connections, coating, roof drainage, weather sealing, doors, windows and electrical continuity. You get a 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Service life runs 20 to 25 years under proper use and maintenance, and that is a design-life statement, not a warranty period.

The honest limits matter just as much. SAMAN does not publish generic occupancy numbers, floor load ratings or wind speed claims for this product, because those values belong to your project calculation, not to a brochure. The published ladder is a planning estimate. The structural quotation is the number you sign.

Double Story Porta Cabin FAQs

How is the price of a G+1 porta cabin calculated?

The planning ladder prices total built-up area across both floors at the published rate input of Rs 1,310 per sq ft with area band adjustments. A 20x10 ft G+1 therefore prices 400 sq ft, not 200. The final price follows the structural quotation for your site.

Do I need a foundation for a double storey porta cabin?

Yes, and it is designed, not assumed. The G+1 structure concentrates both storeys into the ground module supports, so the base and anchoring follow the foundation drawing produced from project structural calculations. Simple levelled ground that serves a single cabin is not automatically enough.

Can I put a G+1 porta cabin on a rooftop?

Only after your structural engineer confirms the slab can carry the stacked loads at the planned position, and only with crane access to that level. Share the building details with your enquiry and we will advise on feasibility before quoting.

How long does delivery take?

Standard delivery takes 7 to 21 working days after order confirmation, plus transit per the Shipping tab. The structural approval step for your configuration is scheduled within the quotation, so the committed programme is stated there.

Can the two floors have different uses?

Yes. Office over office is the most common split, followed by office over store. Each floor runs its own electrical circuits and ventilation, and stacked wet areas are available as optional scope where drawings allow.

Are custom sizes possible beyond the six published options?

Yes. The six-size ladder covers standard footprints from 20x10 ft to 30x20 ft. Other footprints follow the same engineering route against an approved drawing and quotation.

What a Skid-Mounted Porta Cabin Is, and When the Skid Earns Its Cost

Most site cabins move once. A trailer brings the unit in, a crane sets it on its plinth, and it stays there until the project ends. For that duty almost any well-built steel cabin will do. Paying for a heavier base buys a capability you never use.

A skid-mounted porta cabin answers the opposite situation. Here the cabin moves repeatedly, across a project life or across several projects. Every move means a lift, a road journey and a placement. SAMAN therefore builds this configuration on longitudinal steel skid runners, under a heavy frame, with a rough-service floor, protected openings and defined lift, tie-down and service-disconnect points.

The distinction matters commercially. Nineteen of the thirty technical line items in this product differ from our standard cabin specification. They differ for one reason. Repeated handling is a fatigue and damage problem, not a strength problem.

A cabin does not fail on the first lift. It fails slowly. Doors stop closing square. Panel joints work loose. Insulation slumps out of sight. Service connections tear because somebody moved the unit before disconnecting them.

So read this page as a duty decision rather than a size decision. Will the cabin be craned on and off a trailer more than once or twice in its life? If yes, the skid build repays itself in avoided repair and avoided downtime. If no, our standard configurations serve you better and cost less.

What Changes in the Build When a Cabin Is Designed to Move

The chassis becomes the product

The primary structure is a set of longitudinal skid runners. The reference section is 150x75x5 mm MS C-channel or engineered RHS, with wear and nose plates at the ends. Those runners carry transport loads, crane placement and the limited controlled positioning that the approved handling drawing permits.

Runner depth, end geometry and wear-plate extent never come from a catalogue. We finalise them from the unit weight, the support spacing and the handling method your project will actually use. That is why our enquiry asks how the cabin will move before it asks anything about the interior.

Above the runners sit cross-members and anti-racking bracing, referenced at 100x50x3 mm channel or RHS, with reinforced lift and tie-down zones. Racking is the specific enemy here. A cabin twists on a trailer bed, then twists again on the slings. A frame that resists that twist keeps its openings square for years longer.

The envelope suits handling, not only weather

The exterior shell is 1.6 mm corrugated MS or PPGI. We select that gauge for impact and repeated handling rather than for the lowest weight. Where a site will need maintenance access, we fit removable panels instead. Field-cutting a shell creates an unsealed edge, and on a cabin with fifteen moves still ahead of it that edge never behaves again.

Inside, the standard liner is 0.50 mm pre-painted metal or impact-resistant fibre-cement board. We prefer the metal liner on frequently moved units for a plain reason. Board joints loosen under road vibration, and a loosened joint is visible, annoying and awkward to repair on site. Panel joints and service trims allow inspection and tightening after a move rather than replacement.

Wall insulation is 50 to 75 mm mineral wool. Roof insulation runs 75 to 100 mm. Both are retained mechanically so they cannot slump in transit. Slumped insulation is the classic hidden failure in relocated cabins. Nothing looks wrong from outside. The room simply gets hotter every year.

The floor takes the abuse

Floor duty is heavier in a relocated cabin than in a fixed one. The cabin flexes during handling, and the people using it usually arrive in site boots.

The floor base is a heavy MS plate, or 24 mm cement-bonded board on a stiffened grid. The finish is 3 mm chequered plate, or a 2 to 3 mm heavy commercial PVC or epoxy system. Chequered plate suits stores, workshops and high-traffic welfare use. Commercial PVC over a rigid deck suits office variants where appearance matters.

Tell us at enquiry where a machine, a battery bank or a heavy cabinet will stand. The deck then receives a reinforced pad, rather than an apology later.

Openings sit around the structure, not through it

Windows stay smaller than on a fixed cabin. We position them away from high-stress skid and bracing zones, and add guards where exposure warrants them. Doors are heavy assemblies in reinforced frames. A door frame that racks by a few millimetres becomes the first thing a site notices and the last thing anybody wants to fix in the field.

We specify double-leaf access where equipment or furniture passes through regularly. Glazing restraint appears on the inspection list after every relocation, rather than being left to memory.

Services are designed to be disconnected

Competitors do not discuss this part at all. A frequently moved cabin gets clearly labelled external service connection zones. Site utilities then disconnect and cap without anybody pulling on internal distribution.

We secure ventilation and air-conditioning fittings against road vibration. Before a move, the relocation procedure removes or restrains AC outdoor units, condensate lines and external accessories. Plumbing arrives only when you order it, and the same principle governs it. The interface sits outside, labelled and accessible, so the disconnect takes minutes and damages nothing.

Lift, Tie-Down, and the Rule That Protects Your Investment

A skid base is a lifting and restraint system. It is not permission to tow the cabin behind a vehicle. It is not permission to drag it across a yard.

We say that plainly for a reason. The market uses the phrase "skid-mounted" loosely, and a buyer who reads it as towable will damage an expensive asset on the first attempt. The runners suit lifting, transport and controlled positioning. Any permitted skid movement on site happens by winch or rollers, only where engineered, and only where the approved handling drawing shows it.

Three rules travel with every unit:

  • Lift only from the engineered lift and support points on the drawing.
  • Restrain only at the designated tie-down points, using the specified transport restraint.
  • Support the cabin under the skid runners on the trailer bed, never at mid-span.

That last rule prevents the most expensive avoidable failure we see. A unit supported at mid-span sags between its supports. Months later the sag shows up as doors that bind and joints that leak.

Moving the Cabin: Before, During and After

The sequence below comes from the specification document. Read it before your first move rather than after it.

Before the lift. Disconnect and cap electrical and any plumbing services at the external connection zone. Remove or secure the AC outdoor unit and its condensate line. Secure or remove external accessories, which usually means signage, lights, antennas, vents, step units and any projecting fixture. Lock all doors and windows. Secure loose items inside, because road vibration finds whatever you left on a shelf.

During the lift and transport. Use certified lifting gear and lift vertically from the engineered points. Restrain the unit at the designated tie-down points, with support under the runners. Confirm the route for width and height restrictions before the vehicle leaves, particularly for the 12 ft wide body.

After placement. Inspect before the cabin returns to service. Check that doors open, close and lock properly, and check hinges, frames and seals. Check windows the same way, plus glass and latch condition. Inspect the roof, gutters and downpipes, and confirm drainage still runs clear. A move disturbs drainage more often than anything else. Check that external and internal fasteners, brackets and fixings remain secure. Then reconnect services.

None of that is difficult. Sites skip it often enough that we print it here instead of assuming.

Skid-Mounted or Knock-Down: Two Ways to Move a Cabin

Both configurations answer the same question, and they answer it differently.

A skid-mounted cabin moves as one finished unit. It arrives working and it leaves working, so a move costs you the lift, the road journey and the placement. It does need crane access at both ends, and a route that takes the full body width. Choose it when moves are frequent, when downtime is expensive, and when access at both ends is good.

A knock-down cabin travels as components and goes back together on site. It reaches positions a crane cannot serve, and it rides in ordinary vehicles. Every move then costs assembly labour and time. Choose it when access binds harder than speed does.

If your sites vary, decide on the worst access you expect rather than the typical one. That is the move that decides whether the cabin arrives at all.

What to Put in Your Enquiry

A skid enquiry moves fastest when it carries the handling facts, not just the floor area. Include these points and your quotation comes back specific:

  • How often the cabin will move, and over what kind of distance
  • The lifting equipment available at both ends, and whether crane access is confirmed
  • Trailer type available, and any known route width or height restriction
  • Floor duty, including machinery, battery banks or heavy storage and their positions
  • Opening schedule, marking any door that must take equipment through it
  • Electrical load points, AC requirement and whether you need plumbing
  • Receiving-end site conditions, including ground bearing and approach

If the move plan is still undefined, say so. We will quote the base skid build and mark the handling-dependent items as options. Your budget then stays honest while the logistics settle.

Delivery, Freight and Site Readiness

Standard production runs 7 to 21 working days from confirmed order. A fixed-price quotation reaches you within 48 hours of a complete enquiry. Cabins ship from our Bengaluru and Greater Noida units.

Freight follows the published trailer ladder in the Shipping tab. Your site needs a level, load-bearing base, clear approach and turning room for the trailer, working space for the lift, and a power point for the hook-up.

For a cabin that will move again, plan the receiving position with the next move in mind. A unit placed where a crane cannot reach it a second time has quietly become a fixed building.

Exposed coastal or chemical-adjacent duty deserves a separate conversation. Repeated handling and an aggressive atmosphere together are harder on a coating system than either alone. Our galvanized iron porta cabin page covers the corrosion side of that decision.

Quality, Warranty and Honest Limits

Every cabin passes pre-dispatch inspection. The checks cover dimensions, member and panel identification, connections, coating, roof drainage, weather sealing, doors, windows and electrical continuity. SAMAN POS India Private Limited operates ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015 and ISO 45001:2018 certified management systems. The company has delivered 500+ projects for 3,000+ customers across 15+ states from two owned factories.

The commercial warranty reads the same on every SAMAN page, because it comes from one controlled source: 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Relocation damage, misuse, site services, consumables and unapproved alterations sit outside that scope. On a product built to move, that boundary matters more than usual. Plan each lift with competent riggers and to the approved drawing, and the exclusion stays theoretical.

Service life runs 20 to 25 years under proper use and maintenance. That is a design-life statement, not a warranty period. On a relocated cabin the maintenance half of the sentence carries real weight.

We publish no lifting capacity, safe working load, safety factor, weight or permitted number of relocations. Those values belong to the approved handling drawing for your unit and its stated move method. A website figure would be a guess dressed as an engineering number. Where a fire criterion governs your site instead, our fire-rated porta cabin works from tested assemblies rather than from this build.

Skid-Mounted Porta Cabin FAQs

Can the cabin be towed or dragged?

No. The skid runners suit lifting, transport on a trailer and controlled positioning. Towing and dragging are not permitted. Any on-site skid movement happens by winch or rollers, only where engineered, and only where the approved handling drawing shows it.

How many times can it be relocated?

We publish no number. The honest answer depends on the move method, the rigging discipline and the inspection routine. What we do publish is the build that makes repeated moves survivable, and the inspection list that keeps them that way.

Do I need a crane at both ends?

For a standard lift, yes. No price on this page includes crane hire, and access for the lift remains your project's arrangement. Confirm crane access at the receiving end before the cabin leaves. A unit nobody can set down cannot be delivered.

What is the difference from a standard porta cabin?

Nineteen of thirty technical line items. In practice you get a skid runner chassis, anti-racking bracing, a rough-service floor, a transit-tolerant liner, mechanically retained insulation, reinforced door frames, protected openings and an external service disconnect zone.

Is the price higher than other porta cabins?

Yes, deliberately. At Rs 1,750 per sq ft at the reference size this is the highest published rate in our porta cabin range. The chassis, floor and interior all carry handling duty. For a cabin that will not move, a lighter configuration costs less and serves you better.

Can I order it with a toilet or an office fit-out?

Plumbing and fit-out are optional scope, and both belong at drawing stage. On a frequently moved unit the service interface positions matter more than the fittings themselves. Send us the move plan alongside the fit-out you want.
