What \\"knock-down\\" means, and what it does not

Knock-down describes how the cabin is delivered and put together, not what it is made of or what duty it is built for. The cabin arrives as an engineered kit: numbered structural members, a schedule of insulated panels, a gasket set, a fastener schedule and the sequence they go together in. A crew assembles it on your site. When the job ends, the same sequence runs backwards and the components are inspected, repacked and moved.

That is worth separating from two things it is regularly confused with, because the confusion is in the market rather than in the buyer.

The first is a folding or expandable unit. Those arrive as one hinged assembly that opens out. Nothing is bolted together on site, and nothing comes apart into components. It is a different mechanism with a different price and a different set of limits.

The second is a cabin that moves whole. A finished module can be lifted onto a trailer and set down somewhere else, and for many sites that is the better answer because nothing has to be dismantled at all. The skid-mounted configuration is built for exactly that duty, with heavy runners and engineered handling points, and it stays a single unit throughout. If your cabin has to move often but can travel whole, that is the route to look at rather than this one.

So the question this page answers is narrow and specific. Should the cabin arrive finished, or should it arrive as parts? Everything below is about what changes when the answer is parts.

What is actually in the kit

Suppliers describe products as flat-pack without ever saying what arrives. Here is what the specification defines.

The structure comes as segmented bolted base rails, referenced at 100x50x3 mm channel segments, joined through engineered splice plates and bolts. Base cross-members at 75x40 or 50x50 are numbered and bolted to those rails with cleats. Corner and wall posts are referenced at 50x50x2 mm SHS with bolted corner plates. The top rails are 50x50x1.6 mm SHS or formed rail, connecting to the posts through repeatable bolted nodes. Roof secondary members are 50x50x1.6 mm or engineered equivalents with bolted splice details.

One honest qualification belongs here rather than in the small print. Bolt size, bolt grade, hole tolerance, bearing and slip requirements are connection-design items. They are documented for your project, not fixed at catalogue level, because they follow the loads and the configuration you order. Any supplier quoting you a universal bolt grade for every cabin is telling you something about their process rather than about your building.

The floor arrives as modular cassettes on a 50x50x2 mm frame reference, carrying 18 mm cement-bonded board panels, with a 24 mm option where the duty is higher. The cassettes are sized for handling, and joint strips keep the walking surface continuous while still allowing the floor to be opened later. The finish is 1.5 to 2.0 mm commercial vinyl with removable threshold and joint trims, detailed so that module joints can be opened without destroying the whole floor covering.

The envelope arrives as demountable insulated panels. Walls are 50 mm PUF, PIR or mineral-wool sandwich panels, typically with 0.5 to 0.8 mm pre-coated GI or GL facings. Roof panels run 60 to 80 mm with removable flashings and sealed fasteners. Core type is selected against the thermal or fire requirement you state, and mineral wool is used where non-combustible construction is required. Insulation is encapsulated inside the panels, so assembly never depends on loose infill being packed correctly by whoever is on site that week.

Openings arrive as modules. The door is a pre-hung door and frame cassette that fixes mechanically to a structural opening and comes off again as a unit. Windows are pre-glazed aluminium cassettes with replaceable perimeter gaskets, mounted to framed openings so nobody has to cut a panel to fit one. Ventilation, louvers, exhaust and air conditioning provisions are bolt-on service panels with factory-planned cut-outs.

And the kit includes the instructions that make the rest of it work: the numbered member schedule, the panel schedule, the gasket set, the fastener schedule and the assembly and torque sequence.

Why the interior is built the way it is

The interior face of a knock-down cabin looks plainer than a fitted-out finished cabin, and that is deliberate rather than a saving.

A factory-finished sandwich-panel face is specified as the internal skin, in pre-coated metal. The reason is that fragile interior layers do not survive repeated assembly. Board linings crack at the fixings, joints open, and the surface that looked good on day one looks poor after the second cycle. A panel face takes handling. Where decorative lining is ordered, it is clipped or screwed on in removable modules rather than wet-jointed, so it comes off cleanly instead of being destroyed on the way out.

The service ceiling follows the same logic. Ceiling panels stay accessible to wiring and connectors, and any additional ceiling is designed for repeated removal rather than being sealed in place.

What the site has to do

This is the part the category leaves out, and it is the part that decides whether a knock-down cabin is a good decision for you.

Start with the ground. The kit is assembled in position, which means the position has to be right before assembly starts, not adjusted afterwards. A level, compacted, load-bearing base is not a nicety here. A frame assembled out of level will fight you at every bolted node, and panels will not close cleanly onto a racked frame.

Then access, and this is usually the reason a buyer is on this page at all. Components have to reach the assembly position. That is a genuinely lower bar than getting a 40 ft finished cabin there, which is the whole point, but it is not zero. Panels are large flat objects. Base rails are long. The wider kits, particularly at 12 ft, have wider floor and roof cassettes that need more hands or light lifting equipment rather than simply more time.

Then the crew and the programme. Assembly is a sequenced job with a defined order and defined torques. It is not a task to hand to whoever is free that afternoon. The frame goes up with temporary bracing and stays braced until the panels close it. On a 40 ft kit there are more splice nodes to set, align and torque than on a 20 ft one, and that difference is real time on site.

What the site does not have to supply, in the normal case, is welding. The specification states that no site welding should be needed for routine planned assembly unless specifically stated for your configuration. That takes hot-work permits, welding power and welder availability out of your site plan, which on a live industrial or occupied site is often worth more than the steel it saves.

Sealing, and why field cuts are refused

A knock-down cabin is a sealed envelope made of parts that are designed to come apart. Those two facts pull against each other, and sealing is where the tension is resolved.

Joints, corners, roof laps and penetrations use corrosion-compatible fasteners with EPDM, butyl or approved sealants and flashings. No unsealed field cut is accepted. That is not a preference. A cut made on site through a sandwich panel exposes the core, breaks the facing, and creates an edge that cannot be sealed to the same standard as a factory edge, and it will be the first place that leaks at the next reassembly.

This is why ventilation penetrations are concentrated in replaceable service panels rather than being spread wherever a duct happens to land. If a service position changes, a service panel is changed. The rest of the envelope is untouched. Major field cuts in sandwich panels are avoided specifically to preserve reuse and sealing, and that constraint should shape your services layout at enquiry rather than being discovered during installation.

Where plumbing is specified, and it is optional on this product, connections and traps are made accessible so the system can be drained before disassembly. Wet panels are inspected before repacking. A panel that has sat against a leaking trap for a season is not a panel to bolt back up on the next site.

Reuse is a condition, not a promise

The commercial appeal of a knock-down cabin is that you can use it again. That is true, and it is conditional, and the conditions are worth reading before the appeal is priced into your business case.

Reuse depends on inspection. Members, holes, fasteners, panels and seals are all checked between cycles. Bolt holes elongate if a frame has been forced into alignment. Fasteners fatigue. Gaskets take a compression set and stop sealing. Panel facings dent, and a dented facing at a joint line is a leak path.

The specification is explicit about what happens when something fails that inspection: damaged components are replaced rather than forced back into tolerance. That sentence is the difference between a system that can genuinely be reused and one that merely can be taken apart. A cabin reassembled from components that were bent back into shape is a cabin that will leak, rack and disappoint, and it will do so on the site where you needed it most.

Plan for a consumable element, then. Gaskets and sealants are the usual replacements. That is not a defect in the product; it is what a demountable seal is.

Where a knock-down cabin is the wrong answer

Two cases, stated plainly, because sending the wrong buyer down this route helps nobody.

If the cabin is going to one position and staying there for its service life, you are paying for connections you will never undo. A standard welded build is simpler, faster to install and cheaper. The full porta cabin range sets out those options against each other.

If the cabin has to move repeatedly but can travel whole, dismantling it every time is the expensive way to solve that problem. A unit engineered to be lifted and trailered as one piece is the better route.

There is also a case where knock-down is right but something else governs the specification. On coastal or chemically aggressive sites, where the same components will be reassembled outdoors more than once, corrosion behaviour at every cut edge, fastener and joint matters more than the assembly method, and the galvanized iron porta cabin is the better starting point for that conversation. Where sanitation has to sit inside the same footprint, the porta cabin with toilet is the configuration to look at, and the wet-area detailing there is designed around permanence rather than repeated demounting.

Choosing between the six sizes

Six sizes publish. The specification is costed against the 20x10x8.5 ft reference at Rs 1,280 per sq.ft. The other five derive from that input through the area-band adjustment, which is why the rate per square foot falls as the unit grows.

What we need to quote

A useful quotation for a knock-down cabin needs more than a size, because the assembly is half the job:

  • The size you want, and the access constraint that led you to a kit in the first place
  • The delivery route and the assembly position, including gate widths, turning space and any level changes components have to pass
  • Whether you expect to dismantle and reassemble, and roughly how often
  • Your thermal or fire requirement, which selects the panel core
  • The opening schedule: doors, windows, louvers and service penetrations, with positions
  • Electrical scope, air conditioning provision and any plumbing requirement
  • The base you intend to assemble on, and who is preparing it
  • Whether you want SAMAN to assemble, or your own contractor will

The last one changes the quotation most. Tell us early.

Delivery, warranty and service life

SAMAN POS India Private Limited manufactures under the SAMAN Portable brand. Our factories are in Bengaluru and Greater Noida, so units for southern and northern projects are built at the nearer plant. The company was founded in 2009 and incorporated in 2019, with over 15 years of experience. We have a team of over 200, and more than 500 projects and 3,000 customers across over 15 states. We manufacture rather than resell.

A fixed-price quotation is issued within 48 hours of a complete enquiry. Delivery runs 7 to 21 working days, depending on size, configuration and the current build queue. Office hours are Monday to Saturday, 09:00 to 20:00 IST. GST is 18% and the HSN code is 9406.

Warranty is stated as follows: 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Warranty scope and exclusions are confirmed in the final quotation. On this product one exclusion deserves stating in advance rather than being discovered later: damage arising from disassembly, transport and reassembly sits outside the agreed scope unless it is explicitly included, along with misuse, site services, consumables and unapproved alterations. Service life is 20 to 25 years under proper use and maintenance. That is a design life, not a warranty period, and on a demountable product it assumes the inspection and replacement discipline described above is actually followed.

Common questions

Can I assemble it myself?

You can have it assembled by your own contractor, and many buyers do. It is not a domestic flat-pack exercise. The build follows a defined sequence with specified torques and temporary bracing, and the work should be done by people who read structural drawings. We will supply the sequence, and we will quote the assembly if you would rather we did it.

How many times can it be taken down and put back up?

We do not publish a cycle count, because an honest one does not exist independently of how the cabin is handled. Reuse is governed by inspection, not by a number. Members, holes, fasteners, panels and seals are checked each time, and anything outside tolerance is replaced rather than forced.

Is this the same as a foldable or expandable cabin?

No. A foldable unit is one hinged assembly that opens out. This is a set of components that bolt together and come apart. Different mechanism, different price, different limits.

Why is it not much cheaper than a normal cabin?

It is not primarily a cost-saving product. A bolted build carries more connections, more panel interfaces and more sealing detail than a welded one. What you buy is access and reuse, not a lower cabin price, and the site assembly cost sits on top of the figures published above.

Will it be as weathertight as a welded cabin?

It is designed to be, through gasketed and flashed joints rather than continuous welds, and that is why the specification refuses unsealed field cuts and puts seals on the inspection list between cycles. A demountable seal is a maintained item in a way a weld is not.

Do you supply just the kit, without assembly?

Yes. That is the default, and it is what the published prices cover. Assembly is quoted separately, either by us or by your contractor.

What makes a shop cabin a shop, and not a cabin you sell from

Most portable cabins in India are one product with several labels. The same box is offered as a site office, a store, a guard room and a shop, and the only thing that changes is the description. This page is about the version where the building itself is different.

The difference starts at the wall your customer meets. A retail unit is planned around a large service opening: aluminium glazing with a lockable counter opening, sized and positioned for how you actually serve people. That opening is framed and weather-sealed into the chassis while the frame is being fabricated, not cut into a finished cabin afterwards. Around it sit the things a trading unit needs and an office does not: a staff or customer door chosen for your trading pattern, a lockable service shutter that closes the unit overnight, an interior specified as a customer-facing finish, and power points positioned for signage and equipment rather than for desks.

Everything below follows from that. The structure, the panels and the electrical work are the same disciplined build as the rest of the range. What changes is the front, the security, the finish and the layout, and those four things are what you are paying the difference for.

The frontage decision

This is the decision that most affects how the unit trades, and it is the one no competitor in this market publishes in any detail.

Start with how the transaction happens. If your customer stays outside and you serve through an opening, the counter opening is the product: its width, its sill height, how it locks, and whether the glazing beside it is there to display stock or simply to let light in. If your customer comes inside, the door becomes the primary opening and the glazing becomes a shopfront rather than a service point. Those are different buildings with different opening schedules, and choosing between them at enquiry is far cheaper than changing it later.

Then consider closing time. A shutter is not an accessory bolted on at the end. Its fixing points, its housing and the reinforcement around the opening are part of the opening design, which is why the specification treats the door and shutter as one assembly. A unit that is secured properly at night is a unit whose opening was planned to be secured.

Then the signage and power. Retail equipment is not office equipment. A chiller, a display fridge, a fryer, a card machine and an illuminated sign each have their own position and their own load, and they are coordinated with the approved electrical drawing rather than added to whatever sockets happen to be there. Tell us what you will plug in, and where, before the drawing is issued.

What the interior is specified for

The interior of a retail cabin takes a different kind of wear from an office, and the specification reflects that.

Interior walls are 8 to 12 mm plywood with laminate, or 6 to 8 mm HPL panels. The ceiling is an 8 mm decorative board or a 4 mm ACP ceiling. Underfoot, an 18 mm Bison or marine-grade floor board carries a 3 to 4 mm LVT or SPC finish, or a 2 mm commercial vinyl. Those are surfaces chosen to be cleaned repeatedly, to take trolley wheels and dropped stock, and to still look like a shop after a year of it. A site office lining would not.

Insulation is 50 mm glass wool in the walls and 75 mm in the roof. That matters more in a shop than in a store room, because a customer-facing unit is usually occupied through the hottest part of the day with an opening that spends a good deal of time open.

What the site has to prepare

This is the section the category leaves out entirely, and it is the one that most often decides whether a delivery goes well.

The base comes first. The unit arrives complete and is set down in position, so the position has to be ready. A level, compacted, load-bearing base is the requirement. It does not have to be a concrete raft in every case, but it does have to be level and it does have to take the load without settling unevenly, because a unit set down out of level will show it at the door and at the shutter before it shows it anywhere else.

Access comes second, and it is worth checking before you order rather than on the morning of delivery. The smaller sizes travel on a 20 ft trailer; the 30x10 and the 40x10 need a 40 ft trailer. What the vehicle needs is a route in, room to turn, and space beside the final position to set the unit down. Overhead clearance matters as much as width. Where a crane or other lifting equipment is needed, that is arranged and quoted for your site rather than assumed.

Services come third. Power to the unit is your connection; the distribution board, protection and internal circuits are ours. Where the layout includes a sink or handwash point, water supply and drainage to the unit are site scope. Confirm what exists at the position before the layout is finalised, because moving a wet point after the floor is laid is not a small change.

Branding, colour and finish

The exterior colour and coating system are project-selected, and the finish schedule confirms substrate preparation, compatibility, touch-up and the maintenance appropriate to the exposure category. In practice that means a franchise or brand colour can be matched, and the way it is applied and maintained is agreed rather than assumed.

Two honest limits belong here. First, colour matching on a coated steel substrate is agreed against the approved finish schedule, not against a printed swatch held up to a wall. Second, coastal, industrial and heavy-traffic roadside positions are different exposure categories, and the maintenance interval that keeps a brand colour looking right is not the same in each. If the unit is going somewhere aggressive, say so at enquiry: a galvanized iron porta cabin may be the better substrate to start that conversation from.

What a portable cabin shop gives you on a leased plot

Most retail positions in India are not owned outright. They are leased, licensed for a season, allotted on a forecourt, or held on a plot the owner may want back at short notice. That is the situation this build is designed around, and it is where a portable cabin shop earns its cost against a permanent structure.

The unit is set down on a prepared level base rather than founded into the ground. Nothing about it is poured. Engineered lifting and handling points and support locations are provided for each transportable module, so the shop can be lifted and relocated later, moved to the approved lifting, support and transport drawing rather than improvised on the day. If the lease ends, the shop leaves with you and the plot goes back as it was.

Two honest qualifications belong with that. First, relocating is a planned operation involving a trailer and, depending on the size and the position, lifting equipment. It is quoted for the move; it is not included in the purchase. Second, a unit that has been set down, connected and traded from for a year is not a piece of furniture. Services are disconnected, the base at the new position is prepared in advance, and the approved drawing governs the lift. Plan the second move when you plan the first and it is a straightforward job. Discover it on the last day of a lease and it is not.

Compliance is yours, and it is worth knowing early

No prefab manufacturer in this market publishes anything about the permissions a portable shop needs, which is odd, because it is one of the first questions a first-time retailer asks.

The short version is that the building being movable does not remove the obligations that come with trading from it. Registration under the relevant state Shops and Establishments Act, any trade licence your municipal body requires, and any permission needed to place a structure on the plot or forecourt you have in mind are all yours to obtain, and they vary by state and by municipality. We supply the unit, its specification and its documentation. We do not obtain permissions, and any supplier who implies otherwise is worth a second question.

Food service deserves its own line, because it is where the boundary of this product sits. If you intend to prepare or serve food, FSSAI registration or licensing is a separate requirement and is entirely yours. More importantly for your specification: food-service exhaust and plumbing equipment is outside this product\'s baseline unless it is separately specified. What the shop and kiosk build includes is provision - an exhaust or duct provision, a fresh-air opening, a sink or handwash point, water and waste connections and equipment connection points according to your layout. That is provision for equipment, not a fitted commercial kitchen. If your business is a cafe, a restaurant or a food outlet rather than a shop that happens to sell something edible, the container cafe range is built around that duty and is the better place to start.

Where a shop cabin is the wrong answer

Three cases, stated plainly.

If nobody buys anything at the wall, you do not need this build. A cabin for staff, storage, supervision or site administration is a simpler and cheaper product, and the retail frontage package is money spent on an opening you will never serve through.

If your business is food preparation at any scale, the point above applies. Provision is not a kitchen.

If staff will spend a full working day in the unit and there is no toilet within reach of the position, sanitation is not a detail to solve afterwards. A porta cabin with toilet puts a wet area inside the same footprint and details it properly, and on a retail plot with no facilities that is often the more useful configuration than a slightly larger selling floor. The full porta cabin range sets the options out against each other.

Choosing between the six sizes

The specification is costed against the 20x10x8.5 ft reference. The rate per square foot falls as the unit grows, which is why comparing a 10x10 against a 40x10 on headline price alone reads the value wrongly.

Standard, optional, custom and excluded

Standard: the MS structure with its base frame, stiffeners, floor frame, top frame, roof stiffeners and corner and wall posts; engineered lifting and handling points; corrugated MS exterior walls and roof; the plywood, laminate or HPL interior and the decorative or ACP ceiling; the Bison or marine-ply floor base with LVT, SPC or commercial vinyl finish; 50 mm wall and 75 mm roof glass wool insulation; the staff or customer door with lockable service counter or shutter; large aluminium service glazing with a lockable counter opening; the electrical installation to the approved drawing, with DB, MCB and RCCB protection, earthing and segregated circuits; corrosion protection matched to substrate; pre-dispatch quality checks.

Optional: air conditioning for the customer zone; exhaust hood and duct provision; sink, handwash and plumbing connections; grills, mosquito mesh, guards and louvers where the opening schedule requires them; additional openings and service panels; project-selected decorative and external finish.

Custom: the layout itself, meaning the front service counter and the separation between staff preparation and storage zones; the opening schedule; equipment positions and their electrical provision.

Excluded unless written into the quotation: interior fit-out and retail fixtures, transport and installation, craneage or lifting equipment, foundations and hardstanding, site power and water connections, any project-specific engineering, drawings or testing, and any permission, registration or licence.

What we need to quote

A shop is quoted from its frontage, not from its floor area, so the useful enquiry looks different from an office cabin enquiry:

  • The size you want, and the plot or frontage width you have to fit it into
  • How you serve: through a counter opening, or across a floor customers walk onto
  • Your closing arrangement: shutter, door, or both, and what has to be secured overnight
  • The opening schedule, with positions: glazing, counter, doors, louvers and any service penetration
  • What you will plug in and where, including chillers, display units, signage and any equipment load
  • Whether sink, handwash or plumbing is needed, and what water and drainage exists at the position
  • Your brand colour or finish requirement, and the exposure at the position
  • The base you intend to set the unit on, who is preparing it, and the delivery access route

The first two change the quotation most. Tell us those early.

Delivery, warranty and service life

SAMAN POS India Private Limited manufactures under the SAMAN Portable brand. Our factories are in Bengaluru and Greater Noida, so units for southern and northern projects are built at the nearer plant. The company was founded in 2009 and incorporated in 2019, with over 15 years of experience. We have a team of over 200, and more than 500 projects and 3,000 customers across over 15 states. We manufacture rather than resell.

A fixed-price quotation is issued within 48 hours of a complete enquiry. Delivery runs 7 to 21 working days, depending on size, configuration and the current build queue. Office hours are Monday to Saturday, 09:00 to 20:00 IST. GST is 18% and the HSN code is 9406.

Warranty is stated as follows: 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Warranty scope and exclusions are confirmed in the final quotation, and misuse, site services, consumables and unapproved alterations remain outside the agreed scope unless explicitly included. Service life is 20 to 25 years under proper use and maintenance. That is a design life, not a warranty period.

Questions shop owners ask

Can I put a portable cabin shop on leased land without a permanent foundation?

The unit is set down on a prepared level base rather than built into the ground, which is exactly why it suits leased and temporary positions, and it carries engineered lifting points so it can be moved again to the approved drawing. Whether your lease and your local authority permit a structure on that plot is a separate question, and it is yours to confirm. We can tell you what base the unit needs; we cannot tell you what your landlord or municipality will allow.

Can you match my franchise colour exactly?

Colour and coating are project-selected and agreed in the approved finish schedule, which is where the match is confirmed against the actual substrate and coating system rather than against a printed swatch. Bring the brand specification to the enquiry and it is agreed before fabrication, not after.

How is it secured at night?

Through the lockable service counter or shutter and the door lockset, both part of the opening assembly rather than added later. Tell us what has to be secured and how the unit is left overnight, and the opening schedule is planned around it.

Can I run a food outlet from it?

You can sell food from a shop. Preparing food is a different scope: the baseline carries provision, meaning an exhaust or duct provision, a fresh-air opening and sink, water, waste and equipment connection points, but not fitted food-service equipment unless it is separately specified. FSSAI registration is yours. If food is the business rather than part of the stock, look at the container cafe range instead.

How is this different from your office cabins?

The frontage, the security, the finish and the layout. The structure and the services discipline are shared with the rest of the range, which is deliberate; a shop should not be a weaker building than an office, only a differently planned one.

What arrives, and what do I still have to buy?

The building arrives complete to the specification above, with its openings, finishes and electrical installation. Shelving, counters, chillers, display units and everything else that makes it your shop is fit-out, and it is quoted separately.

What an accommodation container actually is

An accommodation container is a steel box, fitted out inside so people can sleep in it, that arrives at your site finished and leaves it in one piece. That last part is what separates it from most site housing. A labour shed or a hutment block is assembled where it stands and comes apart when the project ends. An accommodation container is craned on, connected, used, disconnected and craned off.

The name causes confusion, so it is worth being exact. Some of these units genuinely are shipping containers, converted. Others are not containers at all in the freight sense; they are steel modules built to look and handle like one. SAMAN supplies both, and which one you get depends on the width you order. We publish that split rather than blurring it, because the two routes behave differently on site and cost differently to buy.

Two build routes, decided by width

Every shipping container in the world is 8 ft wide. That is fixed by ISO 668, the standard that lets containers stack on a ship and lock into the same twist-locks anywhere. So the moment you ask for a unit wider than 8 ft, a converted container stops being an option.

That single fact organises our whole range.

The 20x8 ft and 40x8 ft sizes are converted shipping containers. We buy a used donor shell and strip it back. We cut out corroded plate and repair it, then cut the door and window openings and frame them properly. After that the unit is insulated, lined and fitted out. When it leaves the works it presents as a new unit: coated, sealed and clean. It is still a used shell underneath, and we say so, because that determines the inspection we do and the repair we price.

The 20x10, 30x10, 40x10 and 40x12 ft sizes are fabricated wide-body units. These we build new from MS corrugated sheet on a purpose-made steel frame. They keep the container form factor and the corner and handling provisions a container has. Nothing about them is second-hand.

Neither route is better in the abstract. A converted 40 ft shell is a genuinely rugged object that has already spent years being thrown around a port. A fabricated wide-body gives you internal width that no container can, and a known history. The right answer depends on your site.

Why width matters more than length

Buyers usually ask about length first, because length is what they can picture. Inside the unit, width decides far more.

At 8 ft external width, the internal clear width after wall build-up leaves room for one bunk run along one side and a walking aisle beside it. That plan works, and it is efficient in transport terms because an 8 ft unit is a normal load. What it will not do is let two people pass comfortably while a third is getting out of a lower bunk.

At 10 ft, the plan flips. Two bunk runs face each other across a central aisle. You are not simply adding beds; you are changing how the room works at shift change, which is the only time it is genuinely busy. At 12 ft, the aisle stops being a corridor and becomes usable floor, so lockers can stand along it without pinching the walkway.

This is why we describe each size by its aisle arrangement rather than by a bed number alone. Two units of the same floor area, one long and narrow and one shorter and wider, are not interchangeable to the people sleeping in them.

What the published rate covers, and what it does not

We would rather be blunt here than have the conversation at quotation stage.

The published rate is for the finished shell. That covers:

  • The structural box, converted or fabricated
  • Nominal 50 mm class insulated wall and roof package
  • Floor substrate and vinyl finish
  • Doors and windows on the approved schedule
  • Basic electrical fit-out: wiring, protection, lights, fan points, sockets
  • Provision for a split AC: the point, the isolator, the condensate route

These are not in the published rate and are quoted separately:

  • Bunk beds and lockers
  • Toilet, shower, basin or pantry fit-out and the plumbing that serves them
  • The split AC unit itself, as opposed to the provision for it
  • The donor container purchase where a conversion is specified as buyer-supplied
  • Transport, offloading, positioning and installation
  • Foundations, plinths, anchors and external site utilities
  • Project-specific structural engineering, and any specialist certificate or third-party approval

A unit specified with bunks, a toilet and a fitted AC sits in a materially higher rate band than the shell. We publish both positions rather than quoting a low shell rate and letting the fitted-out number arrive as a surprise. If you compare our figure against a market listing, check what that listing includes before concluding anything; in our research, most published prices for accommodation containers do not say.

Bunks, lockers and the bed schedule

Bunk beds are excluded from the base rate for a practical reason as well as a commercial one. Bed dimensions, tier count, aisle clearance, egress and space-per-worker requirements all vary by project. A bed layout frozen in a catalogue is usually wrong for the site it lands on.

We plan on the principle of a separate bed per worker. The approved bed schedule for each size is confirmed on the general arrangement drawing, alongside locker positions. It works around the door and window positions rather than being drawn independently of them. Where a client or funder applies its own worker-accommodation standard, that standard governs and we plan to it.

Toilet, shower and pantry

The base unit has no internal plumbing. That is a deliberate boundary, not an omission.

A dry sleeper and a self-contained wet unit are different products. They differ in floor build-up, waterproofing, ventilation and maintenance. Adding a WC to a sleeper is not a small change. It means a cementitious waterproof floor build-up in that zone, CPVC or PPR supply, uPVC waste and vent, external utility stubs and a slip-resistant finish.

Where a wet variant is required we quote it as such. Water tank, pump, sewer or holding tank and site trenching remain separate unless they appear on the quotation. For a larger camp, a dedicated sanitation block usually beats adding a cubicle to every sleeper. We will say so if that is the better answer for your headcount.

Air conditioning, insulation and heat

The nominal 50 mm class insulated wall and roof package is the standard build. Insulation thickness alone does not make a unit comfortable, and we will not pretend otherwise. Whole-wall performance depends on the steel framing behind the panel, the joints, the openings and vapour control. The cooling load that matters depends on occupancy, solar exposure, glazing and climate.

What we supply as standard is the provision for a split AC: the point, the isolator and the condensate route, sized to the cooling load agreed for your project. The unit itself is itemised separately. On a converted shell, roof-mounted or heavy equipment needs reinforcement and leak-testing before it goes on, because cutting a cargo roof is not a neutral act.

Condensation deserves a mention because it is the complaint we hear most about steel sleepers generally. It is controlled by the liner and vapour detail and by real ventilation, not by adding insulation thickness. Fan positions and openable area are planned with that in mind.

Donor condition, openings and reinforcement

This section applies to the 20x8 ft and 40x8 ft conversions.

A used shipping container arrives with a history: corrosion at the floor line, dents, previous repairs, and a cargo floor that may or may not be sound. We inspect the donor shell and record its condition before the build starts, and structural repair is priced against what the inspection finds rather than assumed.

Cutting openings is the part most often done badly in this market. A container\'s corrugated side wall is structural. You cannot cut a window or a wide door out of it and simply frame the hole with angle. The load path has to be re-established with a documented reinforcement frame, with proper headers and jambs. Where the original cargo deck is retained, we repair and seal it and record what was done. Where it is not sound, we replace it.

What a converted unit is no longer

Once a shipping container has been cut open, insulated, lined and fitted out, it is a building module. It is not a freight container any more, and we do not describe it as one.

That has practical consequences you should know before ordering. It is not CSC-plated for international carriage unless a valid plate applies and that has been separately established. It is not certified for stacking loaded, and it is not offered as sea-freight-ready. Road transport is arranged as an over-dimension or standard load depending on the size, and the 40x12 ft unit in particular is an over-dimension load on most Indian roads.

We are explicit about this for a reason. The word "container" carries an implication of certified transportability that a fitted-out unit no longer holds, and buyers have been caught by it elsewhere.

Electrical scope and earthing

The electrical fit-out uses FR or FRLS copper wiring in approved conduit or trunking. Penetrations through metal are protected, and the runs stay separated from water, waste and any LPG or data services. Typical circuit references are 1.5 sq mm for lighting, 2.5 sq mm for sockets and 4 sq mm for AC and high-load circuits. Final sizing follows the connected load, voltage drop and protection coordination on your project schedule.

Protection is by main isolator with MCB, RCBO or RCCB, with labelled neutral and earth bars. The steel frame and exposed conductive parts bond to the site earth, and that earth has to be tested on site. Generator changeover, fault level and the external supply interface follow your approved single-line diagram. We supply the installation; we do not certify your site electrical system.

Site readiness and unloading

The unit needs a level, stable bearing surface at the support points shown on the drawing, not a full slab. What it does need is honest information about access before dispatch. Tell us the turning radius, overhead clearance, gate width and what lifting equipment will be on site when the vehicle arrives.

The lift plan works from finished weight, centre of gravity, sling geometry and marked support points. Forklift handling is only allowed where pockets and capacity are documented. Craneage and unloading are quoted separately, and delivery runs 7 to 21 working days depending on size, specification and location.

Quality checks and handover

Before dispatch we check dimensions, member and panel identification, connections, coating, roof drainage, weather sealing, doors, windows and electrical continuity, with functional checks on what is fitted. On a converted unit the donor-condition record and the repair record form part of that pack.

Handover evidence identifies the approved general arrangement and bill of materials, the material schedule, test records, photographs, outstanding punch items, lifting and service connection data and maintenance points. Where a specialist performance certificate is contracted, it is verified rather than asserted. We do not publish a fire, acoustic, thermal or structural rating for this product, because a rating belongs to a tested assembly and not to a product name.

Choosing between the six sizes

Work in this order.

  1. Width first. Will the crew change shift together? If yes, go to 10 ft or wider. If it is a small resident crew, 8 ft is efficient and cheaper to move.
  2. Then the build route, which width has largely decided for you. Only 8 ft can be a conversion.
  3. Then length, against your headcount and the bed schedule we agree.
  4. Then transport. Check the route before you fix on 40x12 ft.
  5. Then scope. Decide bunks, toilet and AC now rather than after the quotation, because they move the number.

If your requirement is a whole settlement rather than a unit or two, start at the labour colony hub instead. Suppose instead you want maximum beds at the lowest cost per bed, and the units will stay put for the life of the project. Then labour sheds are usually the cheaper answer, because an open hall carries no per-module steel penalty. A relocatable, repeatedly-craned unit is what the accommodation container is for. It is worth paying for only when you will actually move it.

Frequently asked questions

Are these real shipping containers?

The 20x8 ft and 40x8 ft sizes are, converted from used donor shells. The 20x10, 30x10, 40x10 and 40x12 ft sizes are not. No shipping container is made wider than 8 ft, so we fabricate those from MS corrugated sheet on a new steel frame.

The 8 ft units are second-hand. Does the warranty differ?

No. The standard warranty applies to both build routes: 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation.

Are bunk beds included?

No. Bunks, lockers, toilet and pantry fit-out and the split AC unit itself are quoted separately from the shell rate.

Can I move it between sites?

Yes, that is the point of the product. Confirm the lifting points and support locations on the drawing, and inspect frame alignment, connections, seals and electricals after every relocation before the unit is reoccupied.

Can it go on a ship?

Not as supplied. Once cut open and fitted out it is a building module, not a freight container, and it is not offered as CSC-plated or certified for stacking loaded.

What an oil field camp module actually is

An oil field camp module is a single prefabricated building. It houses a working crew on a remote energy or mining location. It is built to be moved once that location is finished with it. It is not a temporary structure in the sense of something disposable. It is a permanent building with a transport plan attached.

The distinction matters commercially. A conventional site building is designed once, erected once and demolished. A camp module is designed for an unknown number of installation cycles. Almost every cost difference between this page and a fixed labour camp block traces back to that one requirement.

SAMAN manufactures these modules at its Bengaluru and Greater Noida works. The company has been building portable and modular buildings since 2009 and was incorporated in 2019. That is over fifteen years of manufacturing experience, across more than 500 projects and 3,000 customers in 15 states.

The six sizes, and how to choose between them

SAMAN publishes six sizes, from 200 to 800 sq ft of built-up module area. Every size carries one approved bed figure. There are no ranges anywhere on this page, because a range is not something you can plan a camp against.

Match the size to the shift pattern, not just the headcount

The common mistake is to divide the crew size by the bed count and order that many modules. On a location running opposing shifts, half the crew sleeps while the other half works. Beds shared across shifts change the arithmetic completely. A twelve-person crew on a strict two-shift rotation may fit into one 40x10 ft eight-bed module plus a supervisor unit. The same crew on a single day shift needs sixteen beds.

Ask the question the other way round: how many people need to be asleep at the same moment, at the busiest point of the campaign? That number, not the payroll number, sets the bed count.

The rate falls as the size rises

Across every SAMAN cluster the rate per square foot degresses with floor area, and this page is no exception. The shell rate opens at Rs 1,550 per sq ft on the 200 sq ft module and falls to Rs 1,250 per sq ft on the 800 sq ft module. The fitted rate moves the same way, from Rs 1,800 down to Rs 1,400.

The reason is not a discount. A larger module spreads the same fixed content, the same skid design work, the same set of service connections and the same handling effort across more floor area. If two smaller modules and one larger module both house your crew, compare the totals rather than the rates, and then add the second pad, the second lift and the second set of service connections that the two-module option brings with it.

When width is worth paying for

Four of the six sizes are ten feet wide. Two are twenty. The ten-foot sizes give a single corridor with bunks along the walls, which is efficient and moves easily. At twenty feet the layout changes in kind, not only in size. The 30x20 ft module gives two separate four-bed rooms off a common lobby rather than one long room. The 40x20 ft module gives a broad space with a central aisle and real clearance between bunk stacks.

Pay for width in three situations. The first is when crews on opposing shifts disturb each other. The second is when the location is remote enough that one larger lift beats four smaller ones. The third is when a single building cuts pad preparation and service connections. Do not pay for it when the module will move often. A wide-body unit ships in sections and is joined on site rather than lifted whole. It also needs a larger crane window and a more level pad.

What the skid actually changes

The floor of every module in this range sits on a heavy steel skid chassis with two runner beams and reinforced cross-members. This is the single feature that separates the product from a fixed camp block, and it changes four things.

It changes the lift. Marked lifting lugs, corner fittings or transport brackets appear only where the signed general arrangement and lifting drawing shows them. The lift plan identifies the finished weight, the centre of gravity, the sling geometry, the support points and whether the lift needs a spreader. We never assume a one-piece lift. Forklift handling needs documented pockets and a documented capacity.

It changes what you may do with the unit on the ground. Do not drag or tow a module. The one exception is a chassis specifically designed for it, and your quotation will say so. This sounds obvious, and live locations ignore it regularly, usually with expensive results for the floor structure.

It changes the fabrication. The superstructure welds directly into the skid, with local reinforcement at door, AC, service and wet-room openings. The factory completes every structural opening and service cut-out, precisely so that repeated moves do not start fatigue cracks at a field-cut edge.

It changes the inspection points. Skid undersides, cut edges, roof drains and wet-area thresholds are where field durability is won or lost. That is where the coating schedule concentrates its attention.

What one relocation cycle actually involves

A move is a sequence, not an event, and pricing a campaign without allowing for it is the most common budgeting error on this product.

The crew first disconnects the module: power isolated at the point, water and waste drained and capped, external service stubs sealed. Loose contents come out. We then confirm the lift plan against the finished weight and the centre of gravity, because a fitted module weighs more than a shell, and slings that suited it empty may not suit it full.

The crane lifts the unit from its marked points onto the trailer, and the crew secures it. At the new location the sequence runs in reverse, onto a pad that has been levelled and checked for allowable bearing before the vehicle arrives.

Then comes the part that is usually skipped. Inspect the seals, the coating on cut edges, the drainage path and every service penetration before the module goes back into service. A module reinstated without that inspection will still work. It will simply age faster than one somebody checked.

Where the hazardous-area boundary sits, stated plainly

This is the most important paragraph on the page for anyone buying for an operating oil or gas location.

The base module is a normal-area building. SAMAN does not describe it as explosion-proof, blast-resistant, intrinsically safe or hazardous-area certified. Nothing on this page should be read as such a claim. The electrical fit-out, the AC provision and the fittings are normal-area equipment.

SAMAN specifies Ex-rated equipment and interfaces only after you supply the area classification and the project safety basis. This page references IEC 60079-0 only where Ex equipment genuinely applies. Your HSE plan governs siting relative to process equipment, muster and fire strategy, and separation distances, not a manufacturer\'s drawing.

If your location requires a certified hazardous-area package, say so at enquiry. We engineer and price it as a separate scope. No figure on this page includes it.

What the shell rate includes, and what it does not

Every size carries two rates, and the boundary between them stays the same on all six.

Included in the shell rate:

  • The module structure, skid chassis and welded superstructure
  • Insulated wall and roof panel, nominal 60 mm, with PPGI faces
  • Interior lining, ceiling and floor finish
  • Weather-sealed steel personnel doors with heavy hinges and positive latching
  • Aluminium windows with insect mesh
  • Fixed lighting, fan points, sockets, distribution board, residual-current protection and earthing
  • AC provision: the external bracket, the electrical point and the protected wall penetration

Quoted separately, and included in the fitted rate:

  • Bunk beds
  • Toilet and sanitary fit-out
  • The split AC unit itself

Excluded from both rates:

  • Ex-rated equipment, gas detection, blast and fire engineering, process interfaces and hazardous-area certification
  • Sanitary holding tanks and site sewer or disposal arrangements
  • Transport, unloading and craneage
  • Foundations, pads, plinths and site infrastructure
  • Generator, fuel and gas systems
  • Statutory approvals
  • Commissioning

An exclusion list is only useful if it is honest, so nothing above is hidden behind a phrase like \\"as applicable\\". If an item is not listed as included, assume it is quoted.

Site readiness before the module arrives

Most delays on remote locations are ground problems, not manufacturing problems. Settle the following before we confirm a delivery date.

  • A level, compacted bearing surface at the pad, plinth or slab contact points, with the allowable bearing confirmed. Anchor positions are frozen before fabrication.
  • Crane or handling access with a standing area and a swing path clear of overhead services. The wide-body sizes need a larger window than the ten-foot sizes.
  • Approach road capability for a trailer of the relevant length, including turning radii and any weight restriction on the last kilometre.
  • A defined electrical supply point, with the fault level, the changeover arrangement and the site earth identified. The steel frame and exposed conductive parts bond to a tested site earth.
  • Water supply and waste disposal for any size with a toilet or pantry. Remote water quality, holding tanks, freeze or heat protection and disposal remain site responsibilities unless expressly included.
  • Corrosion exposure, if the location is coastal or has an industrial atmosphere, because the coating system is upgraded against exposure rather than assumed.

Services on a remote location

Electrical wiring is FR or FRLS copper in approved conduit or trunking. Protected sleeves shield every metal penetration, and the route keeps clear of water, waste, gas and flexible module joints. Typical circuit references are 1.5 sq mm for lighting, 2.5 sq mm for sockets and 4 sq mm for AC and high-load circuits. Final cable sizing follows the connected load, the voltage drop and protection coordination on the approved schedule. This workbook and this page do not certify the installation.

Protection is by main isolator with MCB, RCBO or RCCB devices. Labelled neutral and earth bars, bonding and surge protection follow the supply and the risk assessment. Generator, DG or UPS changeover follows the approved single-line diagram.

Fixture density follows function rather than a standard count. A crew sleeper, a toolpusher unit and a wide-body block have genuinely different loads, and the quantities come from the approved room and electrical schedule. The quotation excludes loose appliances, kitchen equipment, UPS, DG sets and data devices unless it itemises them.

Where a size carries a toilet or a pantry, the wet package covers the WC, shower, basin or pantry manifolds. It also covers water tank and pump provision, uPVC waste and vent, and protected external stubs. Dry crew sleepers carry no hidden plumbing at all. That is deliberate. A concealed wet route in a module that moves is a leak waiting for the second reinstatement.

What happens before the module leaves the works

Pre-dispatch checks cover dimensions, welds and bolted joints, coating, panel fit, roof drainage, openings, and electrical continuity. Fabrication checks cover fit-up, weld continuity, distortion, bolt tightening, sharp edges and coating repair. SAMAN uses IS 2062 or approved equivalent structural steel. Member sizes and support reactions come from the signed structural drawing, not from a nominal standard section.

Handover evidence identifies the approved general arrangement and bill of materials. It also carries the material schedule, test records, photographs, punch items, lifting and service connection data, and maintenance points. SAMAN supplies certified welding procedures, procedure qualification records and non-destructive testing when the contract or QA plan calls for them, and never by default.

This page states fire, thermal, acoustic, structural and hygiene performance figures only where the contracted evidence supports them for the exact assembly supplied. A panel thickness is not a certificate, and this page does not present one as such.

Maintenance between moves

A module inspected between installations lasts markedly longer than one that is not. The service life of SAMAN\'s modular buildings is 20 to 25 years under proper use and maintenance. That is a design life, not a warranty period.

Six checks matter most after each move. Look at the sealed laps and flashings on the roof, and at the drainage path below them. Check the coating on cut edges and skid undersides. Check the door and window seals. Check the tightness of bolted connections. Last, check every service penetration and its gland. Sealant is a weather detail, not a structural repair. Never use it to disguise a poor lap or an unsupported joint. Deburr, protect and reseal any field drilling.

Warranty and commercial terms

SAMAN supplies a 5-year structural warranty and a 1-year finishing warranty as standard. The finishing warranty is extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Delivery runs 7 to 21 working days, and we issue a fixed-price quotation within 48 hours of a complete enquiry. Prices are ex-GST; GST at 18% applies, under HSN 9406 for prefabricated buildings. We quote customisation beyond the base specification separately.

Warranty exclusions follow the signed quotation and handover documents. The warranty does not cover site foundations, utilities, misuse, unauthorised alteration, poor cleaning, blocked drains, missed seal or coating maintenance, or relocation damage, unless we expressly agree otherwise.

What we need in order to quote

A complete enquiry produces a fixed-price quotation in 48 hours. An incomplete one produces questions. The inputs that matter:

  • Location, nearest town and approach road condition
  • Selected size or sizes, quantity, and required delivery sequence
  • Shell scope or fitted scope
  • Crew size and shift pattern, so the bed count can be sanity-checked against the size
  • Whether a hazardous-area classification applies, and if so, the classification document
  • Power supply arrangement at the location
  • Water source and waste disposal arrangement, for any size with a toilet or pantry
  • Expected number of relocations over the life of the contract
  • Any coastal or industrial corrosion exposure
  • Craneage arrangement, and whether SAMAN is to quote it

Related pages in the Labour Colony range

If the crew is not moving, look at prefab labour camps and colony planning for the fixed-block route. If a single-structure shelter is all the location needs, labour sheds sit at a much lower rate per square foot. They serve a different job entirely.

Questions buyers actually ask

Can the module be towed between locations?

No, unless we designed the chassis for towing and your quotation says so. We design these modules to be lifted, not dragged.

Is it suitable for a classified hazardous area?

Not as supplied. The base module is normal-area. We engineer and price an Ex package separately, once you supply the area classification and project safety basis.

How many times can it be moved?

There is no published cycle limit. The answer depends on handling discipline, lifting method, ground conditions and maintenance between moves. What we design in is a welded superstructure tied to the skid, factory-completed openings and accessible inspection points.

Does the shell price include beds?

No. Bunk beds, toilet fit-out and the split AC unit are the three items that separate the shell rate from the fitted rate.

Can we mix sizes on one location?

Yes, and most campaigns do. A common arrangement is one toolpusher unit alongside two or three sleeper modules sized to the shift pattern.

Do you supply a canteen or an ablution block?

Those are separate SAMAN products with their own configurations. Ask at enquiry and we quote them alongside the camp modules.

What a Multi-Toilet Ablution Block Actually Is

An ablution block is a building whose entire job is water. Every surface in it gets wet, every day, and then gets cleaned with something stronger than water. That single fact separates it from every other structure on a labour camp, and it is why the block is designed from the floor upwards rather than from the walls inwards.

Inside, the block carries repeated banks of WCs, showers and washbasins served from one plumbing manifold, with isolation valves arranged so that a bank can be taken out of service without closing the building. The floor starts as a cement or cement-fibre substrate, takes a waterproof membrane with a perimeter upstand, and falls positively to trapped drains. Walls and ceiling use washable, moisture-tolerant liners with sealed corners. Ventilation runs high, above sightlines, and humid air leaves the building rather than sitting in the roof void.

Buyers usually find this page after single toilet cabins have stopped working for them. That is the honest trigger. A camp of thirty people manages with cabins. A camp of two hundred does not, because the problem stops being sanitation and becomes logistics: too many connections, too many drain runs, too many cleaning stops, and queues that form at whichever units sit nearest the accommodation.

Choose the Depth Before You Choose the Length

This is the decision that matters most on this page, and it is the one most quotations skip.

Length adds fixtures. Depth changes the plan, and with it the service strategy, the maintenance access and the plot you need.

A 10 ft deep block is single-loaded. One bank of cubicles runs along one serviced wall, and everything behind that wall is pipe. It is the simplest thing to connect, the smallest thing to place and the cheapest per building. Its limitation is structural to the plan rather than to the steel: one isolation point governs the whole block, so a repair closes the facility.

A 12 ft deep block is double-loaded. Two banks face each other across a central pipe duct, and supply and waste serve both sides from one spine. Each side isolates separately. In practice this is the change that makes a camp\'s sanitation reliable, because maintenance stops being an event that shuts the block and becomes a job done on one half while the other half runs.

A 20 ft deep block adds a dry entry lobby, and enough width for the two sides to be separated and signed independently where the project requires gender separation. It also gives circulation space that stays genuinely dry, which is what keeps the floor safe when a hundred people use the building inside forty minutes.

Work out your depth from how the camp will run, then choose the length from how many people use the block at peak. Doing it the other way round produces a long, shallow building that queues badly and cannot be serviced without closing.

Why We Do Not Publish a Seat Count

Every competitor listing we reviewed publishes a fixture count. We do not, and the reason is not caution.

A fixture schedule follows the headcount that actually uses the block at peak, the shift pattern, the gender split, the water pressure available at the plot, the drainage invert you can reach by gravity, and the ratios written into your client\'s tender and your state\'s site rules. Two 360 sq ft blocks on two projects can carry materially different schedules and both be correct.

Publishing a number would mean publishing one project\'s answer as though it were the product\'s specification. When the tender then asks for something else, the buyer discovers the gap during fabrication rather than during design, and the change is expensive at that point instead of free.

So the block is priced and sold by built-up wet area, and the schedule is set with you before fabrication. What you send us is the peak headcount per block, the shift pattern, the gender split if there is one, your available water pressure and storage, and the level of the drain or tank you expect to connect into. What comes back is a layout with the banks marked and a fixture schedule against it. Approving that drawing on paper costs nothing. Moving a partition after delivery costs time and money.

A Wet Building Is Not a Dry Cabin

The materials are where the difference becomes physical.

The envelope is a nominal 50 mm PUF or PPGI panel, or an MS frame with a moisture-resistant cement, FRP or PVC liner. Cut edges and panel bases are protected from persistent wetting, and absorbent board edges are kept out of floor junctions, shower zones and basin backsplashes, because that is exactly where a dry-cabin build fails first.

Internally the walls take FRP or PVC sheet, glazed or tiled cementitious board, prefinished metal, or another washable moisture-tolerant liner with sealed corners. Ceilings use FRP, PVC, cement board or coated metal, with sealed penetrations. Every one of those choices is made for compatibility with disinfectant and for easy replacement of a damaged panel, not for appearance.

The floor is the part worth reading twice. An 18 to 24 mm cement or cement-fibre board, or a cementitious substrate, carries a waterproof membrane with a perimeter upstand and a positive fall to trapped drains. Membrane continuity is held around pan collars, shower outlets and wall junctions, and wet testing is completed before the final finish wherever the construction method allows it. The finish is safety vinyl, anti-skid ceramic or porcelain tile, an FRP pan, or another approved wet-area surface with sealed coved edges. Falls and thresholds are set so water does not pond and does not run into dry circulation.

Insulation sits behind the wet-side assembly, not in front of it. Closed-cell PUF or PIR class insulation, or a protected mineral-wool system, sits behind the liner with panel cores and edges isolated from direct water. Insulation helps with condensation control, but the waterproofing is delivered by the wet-side assembly and its joints. No insulation product waterproofs a building on its own, and any supplier who implies otherwise is describing a different product.

Humid Air Is What Kills a Cheap Block

Water on the floor is visible and gets dealt with. Water in the air does not, and it is the slower failure.

A block in use is warm and saturated. High-level louvres and frosted openings give natural ventilation while keeping sightlines out, and mechanical exhaust supplements them where the wet load and room volume call for it. Fan quantity and airflow are sized from the cubicle and shower load against the volume of the room, and the exact air-change values are a project decision rather than a number this page invents.

The roof is treated as part of the same system. It is an insulated PPGI or PPGL assembly with a defined slope, gutters and sealed vent and exhaust penetrations, with vapour and condensation treatment matched to your project\'s climate. Roof drainage is kept separate from sanitary drainage. Humid exhaust discharges to a suitable external location rather than into the roof void, where it would otherwise condense on cold sheet and drip back through the ceiling for the life of the building.

The Services, and Why Access Panels Matter

Supply runs in CPVC or PPR, waste and vent in uPVC, with isolation arranged by bank. WCs, urinals, basins and showers connect per the approved fixture schedule, over floor drains and traps, out to your sewer or holding-tank connection.

The detail that separates a block you can live with from one you cannot is access. Concealed pipe zones get removable access panels rather than permanently trapped valves. Partition framing is coordinated with the plumbing so that valves and traps stay serviceable, and reinforcement is placed at manifold, fixture, door and grab-bar positions rather than fixing hardware to thin liner alone. Where the project requires an accessible cubicle, its supports are structural.

Electrically the block runs FR or FRLS copper in approved conduit or trunking, with penetrations protected and wet-area circuits separated from water and waste routes. Protection is by main isolator with MCB, RCBO or RCCB, with labelled bars, bonding of the steel frame and exposed conductive parts to the tested site earth, and surge protection where the supply or risk assessment calls for it. Final cable sizing follows the connected load, voltage drop and protection coordination on your project\'s electrical schedule. This page does not certify an installation and no workbook can.

What the Price Covers, and What It Does Not

This is the part most quotations leave vague. We state it plainly, because it is the difference between two quotes that look Rs 2 lakh apart and are not.

Included in the published block price

  • The wet-block enclosure: base frame, floor build-up with membrane and finish, walls, roof, insulation, internal partitions and doors
  • Wet-area lining to walls and ceiling with sealed corners and service access
  • Internal water distribution and drainage rough-in to a single defined interface
  • Internal electrical: wiring in conduit, protection, lighting, fan and exhaust points per the approved schedule
  • Factory quality checks, dimensional inspection, coating repair and dispatch protection

Not included, quoted separately when you need it

  • Water storage tanks, sewage or holding tanks, STP and septic systems
  • Pumps, pressure sets and geysers
  • Accessible fixtures and specialist ventilation beyond the approved schedule
  • External trenching, buried site networks and the sewer or tank connection itself
  • Foundations, plinths, pedestals and site levelling
  • Transport, offloading, positioning and installation
  • Statutory approvals and project-specific structural or performance engineering

A block quoted with a septic system in it has been quoted with a septic system in it. Nothing on this page assumes otherwise. If a competing quotation is materially cheaper, this list is the first place to look for the reason.

Getting the Site Ready

The block arrives as a finished building. What it needs from you is a place to sit and three things to connect to.

  • A level, stable standing with a defined bearing surface, sized with a working margin around the block
  • Access along the service side for its full length, and along both long walls on a 12 ft or 20 ft deep plan
  • A water supply with confirmed pressure and storage adequate for the peak wash period
  • A drain or tank connection at a level the block can reach by gravity, confirmed before fabrication
  • A power supply with a tested site earth
  • Vehicle access and offloading space suited to the size ordered

The drainage level is the one that catches projects out. A block set too low for its outfall cannot be fixed with plumbing after delivery, so confirm the invert level early and tell us what it is.

Cleaning and Maintenance

The block is built to be cleaned hard. The finishes take disinfectant, the corners are sealed, and the drains are trapped and reachable. What it needs in return is ordinary: keep the floor drains clear, keep the exhaust running, check the access panels and isolation valves periodically, and repair any coating damage at cut edges and thresholds before corrosion starts there.

Blocked drains, missed seal and coating maintenance, poor cleaning practice, unauthorised alteration and relocation damage sit outside warranty. SAMAN supplies a 5-year structural warranty and a 1-year finishing warranty as standard, with the finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Design life under proper use and maintenance is 20 to 25 years, which is a design life and not a warranty period.

What to Send Us for a Quotation

  • Peak headcount using the block, and the shift pattern
  • Gender split, if the project requires separation
  • The size you are considering, or the plot you have available
  • Available water pressure and storage, and the drainage or tank level
  • Delivery location, access route and offloading arrangement
  • Any client tender clause or site rule that fixes your fixture ratios

We return a fixed-price quotation within 48 hours, with the layout marked and the fixture schedule against it.

Questions Buyers Actually Ask

Is an ablution block the same as a portable toilet?

No. A portable toilet is a standalone unit planned by ratio and placed where people are working. An ablution block is one building serving a camp population from a shared manifold, with showers and a wash run alongside the WCs.

Can I get a working room in the same building?

Not in this product. Where you need a duty room and a washroom in one shell, the porta cabin with toilet is the right choice; it keeps a dry working room and puts the wet zone inside the same cabin.

Why does the rate per square foot fall as the block grows?

Because the frame, the roof drainage run and the single service entry are shared across more floor area. A larger block reuses one connection point instead of adding another.

Can two blocks be placed together and connected as one?

Yes, and camps commonly phase it that way. Tell us at quotation stage so the service interface and the isolation arrangement are planned for it rather than retrofitted.

Do you supply the septic tank or STP?

Not in the block price. External tanks, STP and septic systems, pumps and site networks are quoted separately.

How long does delivery take?

Delivery is 7 to 21 working days depending on size and schedule, confirmed at order.

What a Porta Cabin with Toilet Is, and Who Orders One

A porta cabin with toilet is one steel cabin with two jobs. The main body works as a duty room, gate office or crew space. A built-in wet zone carries the WC, urinal and washbasin fittings your layout calls for. SAMAN builds the shell as a standard MS porta cabin and upgrades the wet zone with moisture-tolerant materials, factory plumbing and forced ventilation. You order one unit, receive one delivery, and connect one set of services.

Contractors buy this cabin for construction gates and plant entries. Project owners place it where a small team works a full shift away from permanent buildings. Facility and event teams use the larger sizes as a combined duty room and washroom block. Site welfare rules in most Indian projects expect working sanitation near the workforce, and a factory-plumbed unit is the fastest way to put it there. In every case the buyer problem is the same: people need a place to work and a clean toilet, and the site cannot wait for civil construction.

Many buyers search for this same unit as a portable cabin with toilet. At SAMAN the two names describe one product: the same MS shell, the same wet zone, the same published ladder. Whichever term brought you here, the sections below answer the same set of decisions.

Plan the Layout by Seat Count, Not by Guesswork

Inside the shell, SAMAN plans separated toilet, urinal and washbasin zones according to the seat count you select. A small unit carries one WC zone beside the duty room. Mid sizes add a basin run and a urinal line. The largest sizes carry full cubicle banks with the washbasins placed clear of the door swings. This is the detail that decides daily comfort, so settle it before fabrication, not after delivery.

The working room follows the same logic. A 20x10 ft unit can hold a furnished office room with an internal WC compartment behind a flush door. Where the whole cabin serves a larger crew as a washroom block, the floor gives way to cubicles and circulation space instead. Doors and door swings matter here: waterproof flush doors with privacy fittings close each wet zone, so the working room stays dry and private.

Tell us how many people use the unit on a normal day and what they use it for. The layout drawing comes back with zones marked before you confirm the order, and fabrication follows that approved drawing. Changing a partition on paper costs nothing; moving one after delivery costs time and money.

The Wet Zone Is Built Differently From the Dry Room

Water destroys ordinary cabin interiors, so the wet zone uses its own material set. Walls carry 10-12 mm fibre-cement board with a moisture-tolerant lining and a hygienic finish. The floor starts as an 18-24 mm cement board and takes a waterproof membrane. It finishes in 2.5-3 mm anti-skid safety vinyl with sealed joints, so wash water stays above the membrane and off the steel. The ceiling uses 8-10 mm fibre-cement or washable PVC, which wipes clean and shrugs off humidity.

The dry room keeps the standard porta cabin build: corrugated MS shell outside, insulated cavity, and a clean panel finish inside. Wall insulation is 50 mm mineral wool where required. The roof carries 75 mm glass or mineral wool, which keeps the afternoon heat load down. Both zones sit on one welded MS chassis, so the cabin still lifts, travels and places as a single piece.

Factory Plumbing: What Arrives Fitted, What Your Site Connects

Every wet line is routed at the factory. CPVC pipes feed the fixtures. UPVC lines carry waste to a single outlet point, with traps and floor drains set under the finished floor. Fixtures follow your layout: an EWC or Indian WC in each cubicle, urinals and washbasins where the seat count calls for them, with flushing fitted. A mechanical exhaust fan is standard in the wet zone, supported by frosted aluminium ventilators, so moisture leaves the cabin instead of soaking into it.

Your site keeps a short, clear scope. Bring a water supply line to the cabin, take the waste outlet onward to your septic tank or drainage, and give the cabin a power connection. The table below draws the line exactly, because handover disputes start where scopes blur.

Six Sizes, One Published Price Ladder

SAMAN publishes the complete ladder, so you can budget before you call. The base rate is Rs 1,450 per sq ft at the 200 sq ft reference size. Every other size follows a published area-band rule: smaller floors pay a premium per square foot, larger floors earn a reduction. Prices cover the base cabin specification. Interior fit-out, optional add-ons, transport and foundations are quoted separately.
